articles.title_orig: Scientists discover ghostly, eyeless creature hidden in Chinese cave
articles.title_zh: Scientists discover ghostly, eyeless creature hidden in Chinese cave
articles.content_orig:
A newly identified freshwater cave snail in China is offering scientists a rare glimpse into the little-known aquatic ecosystems hidden beneath East Asia. Published in the journal Subterranean Biology , the discovery represents an important step forward in understanding the region's underground wildlife. Until now, no freshwater cave snails had been documented in China, and the country's subterranean freshwater mollusks had received relatively little scientific attention.
The newly discovered species, Erhaia dijiang , has evolved remarkable features that allow it to live in complete darkness. As a true cave-dwelling animal, it has entirely lost its eyes, with the structures normally associated with vision having fully degenerated. The tiny snail also has a cone-shaped, nearly transparent shell, a delicate body without pigmentation, and long, slender tentacles.
Its unusual appearance inspired a name drawn from ancient Chinese mythology. Researchers chose dijiang in honor of "Di Jiang," a mountain patron god portrayed as a faceless beast in the ancient text Classic of Mountains and Seas (山海经). The connection is particularly fitting because the snail is extremely sensitive to light. During laboratory observations, individuals consistently retreated into dark spaces beneath rocks whenever they were exposed to illumination.
The location of the discovery is just as remarkable as the animal itself. Scientists found Erhaia dijiang at an elevation of 2,062 meters, making it the highest-altitude cave snail yet recorded within the family Erhaiidae. The finding demonstrates that freshwater cave snails can inhabit limestone cave systems at elevations above 2,000 meters.
Life in the Dark Waters of a Mountain Cave
Within its underground habitat, Erhaia dijiang lives among submerged gravel and broken rock in water less than one meter deep. The cave's water temperature stays close to 20°C, providing a relatively stable environment for the tiny mollusks.
Even when heavy seasonal rains increase the flow of water and occasionally wash a few snails out through the cave opening, they have not been observed in nearby streams. Researchers found that the animals remain confined to the cave environment, staying within two meters of its entrance.
Laboratory observations also provided clues about what these elusive creatures eat. The snails were seen feeding on diatoms, microscopic algae that grow on rock surfaces, and they also consumed fish food supplied by the researchers.
Only Three Living Snails Found, Raising Conservation Concerns
Although the discovery sheds new light on China's largely unexplored underground aquatic biodiversity, researchers are concerned about the species' future. They describe its conservation outlook as "far from optimistic."
During the first field investigation in August 2025, the team encountered an exceptionally small number of snails. Despite searching the shallow cave waters, researchers located only three living adults and one empty shell. They found no juveniles, suggesting that the known population is extremely sparse.
The scientists are now urging more comprehensive investigations of cave ecosystems throughout China to uncover additional species and better understand these fragile underground habitats. They also emphasize the need to develop conservation protections quickly for these vulnerable mollusks, which are native to highly restricted environments and could face serious threats before their populations are fully understood.

articles.title_orig: China Stocks Rise on Tech Optimism
articles.title_zh: China Stocks Rise on Tech Optimism
articles.content_orig:
The Shanghai Composite edged up 0.2% to 3,742, while the Shenzhen Component gained 0.6% to 11,870, as upbeat corporate earnings lifted sentiment toward technology stocks.
SpaceX reported net income well above market expectations, while Super Micro Computer also delivered better-than-expected results, helping ease concerns over stretched AI valuations and funding pressures that recently rattled the sector.
Cambricon Technologies (1.2%), Hygon Information Technology (2.1%), Zhongji Innolight (2.5%), Eoptolink Technology (3.1%) and NAURA Technology (2.2%) were among the top gainers.
In contrast, CATL plunged 5.4% after Q3 earnings missed market expectations, as rising costs and other pressures squeezed margins.
Meanwhile, investors continued to assess the stronger economic growth outlook, which gives policymakers more room to delay further stimulus.
However, sluggish domestic investment and consumption continue to pose risks to growth in the absence of broader policy support.

articles.title_orig: Opinion | Burnham’s Britain can learn from Trump in engaging with China
articles.title_zh: Opinion | Burnham’s Britain can learn from Trump in engaging with China
articles.content_orig:
While an IPAC report accurately notes that Britain is woefully unprepared to get relations with China right, the audit’s ideological framing is unhelpful
Getting relations with China right is widely seen as Britain’s epoch-defining challenge. It is also one it is woefully unprepared to face.
So concluded a recent audit by the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (IPAC), which highlighted that top negotiators lacked basic Chinese language skills. More critically, it exposed a deeper deficit: a poor grasp of China spanning political elites and the public alike. This is rooted in a desk-bound classroom sinology rather than a nuanced appreciation and lived immersion.
Yet IPAC’s audit will do little to fix this deficit. Indeed, its ideological framing will deepen it.
The report depicts China as a neo-totalitarian state seeking to engineer the souls of its citizens. It alleges that this coercive ambition extends globally, that Beijing seeks to upend the liberal world order to usher in an era favourable to authoritarian imperialism.

articles.title_orig: Witkoff to present Putin with peace proposal after talks with Zelensky
articles.title_zh: Witkoff to present Putin with peace proposal after talks with Zelensky
articles.content_orig:
US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Volodymyr Zelensky are meeting in Oslo, with relations on the slide between the Ukrainian leader and US President Donald Trump.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said Zelensky had asked Oslo and neighbouring Finland to organise the talks with the US and European allies "at a critical time for Ukraine".
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier rejected as "scandalous" accusations that Ukrainians were dying because the US was withholding intelligence from Kyiv.
He was speaking after Zelensky's top military adviser Serhii Beskrestnov told the BBC the lack of reliable US warnings - including about ballistic missile launches - meant lives were being lost.
"This looks very strange," said Beskrestnov, widely known as "Flash". "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not."
Relations between Kyiv and the US have soured in recent weeks to the extent that Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president, and most recently "for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine".
Zelensky first met the Norwegian prime minister and Finnish President Alexander Stubb, ahead of his talks in person with Witkoff, with Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner taking part via video link.
Støre said the aim of the talks was to steer relations towards "a more constructive path". He told reporters at the parliament in Norway that they wanted to ensure that the war ended diplomatically with a lasting and just peace.
Zelensky took with him to Oslo Ukraine's intelligence chief Rustem Umerov and influential lawmaker Davyd Arakhamia, both of whom had earlier this month held talks in Miami with Witkoff and Kushner.
Those talks were reportedly ended abruptly when the Ukrainian delegation learned that Trump had announced that Moscow would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the US and other markets, bringing to an end American sanctions on Russian diesel exports.
Zelensky had reacted by calling it "a happy birthday present" for Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Ahead of next month's US midterm elections, Trump has blamed Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries for fuel prices which have reached record highs at the pump since the start of the US-led war on Iran.
Speaking before the Oslo talks, Zelensky said he had had a "constructive discussion" with Rubio about the need for US early warnings, missile interceptors and SpaceX's Starlink internet network.
Last week a bipartisan group of US senators called for an urgent investigation into speed restrictions to the Starlink network in Ukraine. Unconfirmed reports on Tuesday said the transfer of more Patriot interceptors - the only effective weapon in shooting down Russian ballistic missiles - had not yet been approved.
Rubio is currently on a visit to India and admitted to reporters that it may be true that Patriot interceptor missiles - the only had not yet arrived in Ukraine, although nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally.
Zelensky was set to join his Norwegian and Finnish counterparts for a press conference after the talks, but Witkoff was not expected to join them, according to the government in Oslo .
It is not yet clear whether Witkoff will travel on to Russia after Oslo, however the Kremlin spokesman said he hoped a meeting with Trump's envoy could be organised in the near future. Dmitry Peskov said "we greatly appreciate the mediation efforts of the American negotiators".
Speaking later on Thursday, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov was quoted by the country's state-run media as saying "we'll see what they [Witkoff and Kushner] offer", but stressed that there would be no political concessions from the Kremlin.
European leaders have expressed concern about recent statements from the US towards Russia, and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke on Monday of "mixed pictures and messages" on the war, adding that he was trying to convince the American government "in total that this is something we have to resolve jointly".
He pointed out that the US had not been paying for the defence of Ukraine since the start of 2025, and Europe and other countries were shouldering the burden.
"It's really a big effort for our budgets, it's really a big thing for the European Union, but we are doing that and we are trying to keep on doing that until this terrible war ends," the German leader told Bloomberg TV.
Asked whether or not Ukraine was a US ally, Vice-President JD Vance has said in a TV interview that Kyiv was "certainly a partner in some ways, but we have some divergent interests from time to time, like for example... I think they should stop bombing Russian energy".
"We don't have a formal alliance as far as I know with Ukraine. They're not in Nato, I don't think they should be in Nato... we're gonna work together on some things, but also we're going to be opposite on some things too."
Russian drone attacks continued on Tuesday unabated. Ukrainian officials said at least 10 people were killed - four in Kyiv and the capital region, another four in the eastern Donetsk region, and two in the central city of Dnipro.
In Kyiv, the operating room of a cardiology institute was hit, injuring one patient, Ukraine's Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky said.
This comes a day after a Russian drone strike killed a toddler in her pram, an 11-year-old girl and another four people near a park café in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.
Zelensky described that attack, in which another 14 people were injured, as "absolute atrocity".
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

articles.title_orig: Man, Woman Executed for 'Indecent Acts' in Mecca Mosque
articles.title_zh: Man, Woman Executed for 'Indecent Acts' in Mecca Mosque
articles.content_orig:
Bangladeshi authorities say they were not informed of the recent execution of two Bangladeshi nationals in the holy city of Mecca until after it had taken place, local media reports.
A Bangladeshi man and woman were executed last Wednesday after being convicted of committing an "indecent act" inside a mosque, according to the Saudi interior ministry. The ministry did not specify the nature of the offending act.
Bangladesh says it has reached out to the Saudi Arabian government to ask for more details about the case.
The two Muslim countries share a close relationship due to their religious affinity and strong economic ties.
More than three million Bangladeshis work and live in Saudi Arabia, mostly in low-paying jobs, and news of the double execution has raised public concern in Bangladesh.
According to the Saudi interior ministry, the two Bangladeshi nationals were convicted and sentenced to death under "tazir", which in Islamic law refers to punishments left to the discretion of the judge.
The ministry statement said they were handed the sentences because of the severity of the offence, and the fact that they violated the "sanctity" of the mosque.
Bangladesh has reached out to the Saudi government about the offences involved and legal proceedings in the case, said state minister for foreign affairs Shama Obaed Islam.
The government would consider next steps, such as the repatriation of the bodies, after getting information from Saudi authorities, Islam said.
She added that the government was committed to safeguarding the welfare and interests of Bangladeshis abroad.
The two executed Bangladeshis were included in a list of prisoners that Saudi Arabia had shared with Bangladesh, upon a request from the Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah - but that list did not indicate that the pair had been sentenced to death, the Daily Star reported.
This is not the first time that foreign nationals have been executed by Saudi authorities.
According to Amnesty International, the country has executed around 100 people this year, many of whom are foreigners convicted of drug offences.
In 2011, eight Bangladeshi men were publicly executed in the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh after they were found guilty of killing an Egyptian.
Earlier this month, Saudi Arabia overturned a death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan man over a comment he had made on Facebook, which had led to him being convicted of blasphemy. That decision came after the case sparked public outcry in Sri Lanka and spurred diplomatic efforts to seek clemency for the man.

articles.title_orig: France is divided over who to blame for and what to learn from weekend riots
articles.title_zh: France is divided over who to blame for and what to learn from weekend riots
articles.content_orig:
"This is not the face of France! You media all focus on the violence and destruction of Saturday's protests. But that's not the majority. It's not 'us'. That's not France!"
Elisabeth was speaking to me in front of a row of smashed shop windows, shattered glass still littering the tree-lined Parisian street. Its walls were daubed with red-lettered graffiti insulting French police and signed with the date of the riots, 17 October.
I'd stopped her and her friend to ask what they thought of what happened on Saturday. Elisabeth was so upset that, when she spoke, she seemed close to tears.
"My friend thinks this is civil war in France but I don't. Saturday is about something else entirely."
But what did happen exactly? Who was behind the riots? While much of the looting seemed opportunistic, the violence looked pre-planned. Why orchestrate it now, after weeks of student protests? And who most stands to gain from the destruction this weekend? Elisabeth wasn't entirely sure.
Different theories are doing the rounds - in and outside France. Black and white answers may be appealing, but the truth is there are many factors at play.
The president of the National Assembly, Yaël Braun-Pivet, has proposed a parliamentary inquiry into the riots and how they were organised.
French intelligence had briefed government circles earlier this month that left-wing anarchist groups were involved in the student protests. Their signature: a capital A, circled in black, was spray-painted on many buildings across France this weekend.
French media have played and replayed a video shot on Saturday showing groups of young men dressed in black, with a black folded kerchief around their face to hide their identity, apparently attacking a number of police vans with what look like large hammers or machetes.
A French intelligence report dated 29 September, published by Le Figaro newspaper, details the "manipulation" of student demonstrations by student unions and political movements aligned with the radical left. It suggests the far-left political movement La France Insoumise (LFI) was relying on violence as an electoral strategy ahead of the 2027 presidential elections.
The mass looting of what's said to be over 3,000 shops and businesses on Saturday appears to have been largely opportunistic, according to French reports. Many youngsters immediately went online trying to sell their stolen wares, including designer trainers. Some didn't bother to cover their faces. Did they feel a sense of impunity?
Online sales platforms now say they'll work with the French authorities to track down as many of the looters as possible. Police say they're examining CCTV and social media footage. President Macron insists all those responsible for violence or theft will be brought to justice.
Suggestions that some were encouraged to join in the violence by social media posts has lead former French Prime Minister Gabriel Attal (a hopeful in France's upcoming presidential election) to call for selected social media blackouts to quell further violence.
Belgium has also been experiencing violent protests these last days. On Tuesday, Belgium's Interior minister Bernard Quintin, warned of the 'TikTokisation' of violence. Footage of riots is widely shared on social media, reaching a large audience of impressionable young people, he said, while also blaming violence on the streets of Brussels and Liege on "known far left groups".
In France, Prime Minister Sebastian Lecornu and his Interior Minister Laurent Nunez have also clearly implicated the "hard left" in Saturday's mayhem - "pouring oil onto the fire," said Nunez. On Tuesday Mr Lecornu spoke of  "insurrections" planned by "small far-left and ultra-left groups".
Previously he'd accused the "far left" of weaponising student demos.
It's something anti-capitalist LFI leader, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who also hopes to become French president, has vehemently denied.
Mélonchon took part in Saturday's planned protest. Politicians from his LFI movement have been present at the student demonstrations since they started a month ago in the socially deprived outskirts of Paris, with demands for better state education for all.
In Saint-Denis suburb on Monday, I met Lisa Cordat, of the FSE student union. She told me that students organised themselves for demos via social media messaging or through student-led organisations. She said it was "insulting" to suggest they were being manipulated or "told to do this, or do that" by politicians.
"Student anger comes from the ground up," says Lisa.
But there is also a palpable frustration amongst many in France at what they see as the politicisation of Saturday's violence. Lina, who is 25, told me: "Politicians are hunting for scapegoats but don't ask why it all happened. The root causes of Saturday. We feel scared and abandoned."
France's leading politicians have indulged in a festival of finger-pointing since Saturday.
The presidential election here in six months' time is hotly contested and the volatility on French streets funneled immediately into France's already febrile politics.
Mélenchon, currently running in second place in most polls, ahead of centrist candidates, accused France's centrist Prime Minister of being "responsible for the chaos" either due to "incompetence or a worst-case strategy."
Mélonchon went on to apparently imply Mr Lecornu may have allowed the violence to unfold, so as to position itself as a "party of order", after Saturday's lawlessness, "that would make people forget his failure in public finances."
France is struggling with spiralling public debt and government borrowing costs.
As for intelligence failures on Saturday, President Macron has demanded explanations and a new policing strategy. France's Interior Minister admitted there weren't enough officers on the streets, despite the nationwide protests being publicised well in advance. Following accusations of heavy-handedness at earlier demos, the police seemed very much out of their depth this weekend.
Of all the presidential hopefuls, it would seem Marine Le Pen of the anti-immigration, National Rally Party gains most politically from Saturday's shocking scenes.
She is already way ahead in opinion polls. Le Pen chose to launch a presidential-looking video address to the nation via social media on Sunday. Dressed formally, behind a large desk and in front of a French flag, she blamed Jean-Luc Mélenchon by name for his associates who "look to throw the country into chaos," she said.
She also accused the Macron government of "running out of steam", meaning that France was "taken hostage between violence and powerlessness".
She ended her video by reminding French voters they'd have the opportunity to "choose a different path" in 6 months time.
Le Pen's party promotes a law and order, closed border message and, like US President Trump and Vice US President JD Vance, has blamed migrants, amongst others, for the chaos in France on Saturday.
Teacher, Mar, complained that Saturday's violence "suits politicians' purpose. It distracts from weeks of legitimate protests for better public services," she said.
"Politicians aren't listening to what the students need, or what teachers need or what the French people want. They're using the violence to election-campaign to become president and to try to make their opponents look bad."
But increasing numbers in France, many amongst the young Gen Z generation, say they have dwindling faith in "the system".
That's something we see echoed in other European countries where mainly youth-led protests erupted - some violently - this weekend in Italy, Portugal and Albania as well as France and Belgium.
These demonstrations are often triggered by spiralling living costs, deteriorating public services and a sense of powerlessness people feel over their own lives.
What can we do as individuals about our rising energy costs caused by wars far away in the Middle East or in Ukraine, many ask?

articles.title_orig: Alberta rejects a move toward independence from Canada in a victory for Carney
articles.title_zh: Alberta rejects a move toward independence from Canada in a victory for Carney
articles.content_orig:
The oil-rich province of Alberta has rejected the pathway to secession and will remain part of Canada, landing a definitive blow to a fringe but loud campaign which sought support from the US.
About three quarters of voters chose to stay in Canada, while one quarter opted to hold a second vote on separation later as of early Tuesday local time, with around 86% of polling locations reporting, according to unofficial results posted by the province.
Monday’s result comes amid a rising tide of patriotism and unity in Canada as the country has rallied against US President Donald Trump’s tariffs and annexation threats.
The Alberta independence campaign, a grassroots effort led by a handful of vocal separatists, was amplified heavily online, and some of its leaders had met with members of Trump’s administration.
The vote had faced concerns of possible foreign interference after Canadian newspaper the Globe and Mail reported Republican operatives had assisted top separatist leaders with their independence bid.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said the vote to remain means that “Albertans and all Canadians will move forward together with renewed purpose and high ambition” in a statement posted to X early Tuesday.
Thomas Lukaszuk, former Alberta politician and founder of the pro-unity Forever Canadian movement, said the result would send a strong message to Trump: “Canada is not up for grabs.”
“We are a solid country that’s united from coast to coast to coast and we stick up for each other,” Lukaszuk told a cheering crowd as the results came in.
The morning after the vote, leading separatist activist Jeffrey Rath told CNN that he was proud that his movement managed to convince roughly a quarter of voters to ask for a referendum.
“We started basically from nothing, a year and a half ago, and we’ve dominated the conversation,” Rath said. “For a fledgling political movement, it was a major victory and a hell of an accomplishment.”
At least one separatist group has not yet acknowledged the loss of the referendum side. The Alberta Prosperity Project, which organized a petition drive for an independence vote earlier this year, said in a statement on X that it awaits “the release of the official count and a careful analysis of the process before drawing conclusions.”
“This isn’t over, Alberta,” the organization added.
Monday’s vote was the first plebiscite of its kind in Canada since the 1995 Quebec referendum, where the predominantly French-speaking province voted against secession by a razor thin margin.
Alberta, a province roughly the size of Texas, has long harbored a fringe independence movement. Separatists there argue that Canada’s federal system underrepresents its population of 5 million in parliament, that Canadian efforts to fight climate change threaten Alberta’s lucrative fossil fuel industry and that Alberta’s conservative politics are often outweighed by the more liberal eastern provinces.
Though separation frequently polled low in Alberta, the movement grew louder after Carney’s Liberal Party won the 2025 federal elections amid a trade war with the United States.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced in May the province would hold a referendum on whether to remain in Canada, or to have a “binding provincial referendum” on independence later.
Over the past two years, secessionist leaders have met with US officials in Washington to try and negotiate support from the Trump administration. Rath, who was part of the group in DC, told CNN last year that Trump’s election in 2024 gave independence activists hope.
“If anybody is going to have the guts to recognize an independent Alberta, (it) would be the Trump administration,” Rath said.
News of the meetings at the time incensed Canadian politicians , who accused separatist leaders of “treason.”
The movement also possesses a Trumpian flavor. Participants at a secessionist rally CNN attended in 2025 donned red MAGA-style “Make Alberta Great Again” hats. A minority even said that Alberta ought to skip independence and become the 51st US state.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has lent support to the separatist cause, saying Albertans are “very independent people” and that the province is a “natural partner for the US” in an interview earlier this year.
Last week, Elon Musk, a Trump ally, urged Alberta, along with other Canadian provinces Saskatchewan and Quebec to separate from Canada in a post to his platform X, saying they would be “better off.”
Smith said she was “very pleased” with the result to remain in Canada in a post to X late Monday local time, but she has previously cautioned against “demonizing” independence supporters.
“We have had, from time to time, these kinds of initiatives flare up,” Smith told CNN in 2025. “And they’re almost always in response to a federal government that’s out of control. But they have all subsided when the federal government got back in its own lane.”
Carney, who grew up in Alberta, nodded to that frustration in a speech in Calgary last week urging voters to reject secession. “The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real,” Carney said.
But, the prime minister said, separation would only “burden” Albertans “with years of deep division and great uncertainty.”
He also made an oblique swipe at the US.
“This referendum comes at the worst possible time,” he said. “The world has become more dangerous and divided. Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us.”

SpaceX shares climbed about 8% in extended trading on Tuesday after the company reported 161% revenue growth for the third quarter, beating Wall Street estimates, with its artificial intelligence business growing ninefold.
On the earnings call, CEO Elon Musk said a merger with Tesla , his automaker, would be a "good idea," adding that the boards of both companies have formed special committees to discuss a tie-up. Tesla reports third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday.

Johnsen attributed the forecast to "increased visibility into our compute contract pipeline over the next six months."
While SpaceX is best known for its reusable rockets, most of its revenue and profit in recent quarters came from the company's connectivity segment, which consists of its Starlink satellite internet service.
Starlink's subscribers base grew to 13.6 million in the quarter, up from 12 million in the prior period.
Total connectivity revenue jumped 69% to $5.25 billion from $3.1 billion a year earlier. Analysts were expecting $4.84 billion, according to StreetAccount. SpaceX jumped into AI with the purchase earlier this year of xAI, Musk's AI lab. The company has been rapidly expanding that business by renting out capacity to Google , Anthropic and others.
AI, which SpaceX now calls "Super Intelligence," has emerged as its largest business. Revenue jumped ninefold to $7.56 billion from $813 million in the same quarter last year. Analysts expected sales of $6.47 billion, according to StreetAccount.
During the third quarter, SpaceX also closed its $60 billion purchase of AI coding startup Cursor.
Meanwhile, SpaceX's launch business was up just slightly in the quarter, with sales rising to $1.77 billion from $1.67 billion a year ago.
Almost all of SpaceX's profit still comes from Starlink. Operating income in the connectivity unit about doubled to $2.37 billion. The AI business swung to a profit of $431 million, while the space division lost $7 million.
Between infrastructure, cloud deals and paying users of the Grok AI models and products, Musk said on the call that annual recurring revenue by the end of next year will be between $500 billion and $1 trillion. SpaceX's launch business generated $1.77 billion in revenue in the third quarter.

He added that SpaceX has a "steady stream of Starship flight attempts" scheduled through the end of this year, and accelerating next year.
The company recently announced plans to build a $100 billion spaceport in Louisiana. SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell said on the call that SpaceX aims to conduct its first launch from the facility by 2029. Musk said the first launch may be possible by the end of 2028.

The data centers are powered by methane gas-burning turbines, installed by SpaceX's AI business.
The NAACP, in its suit, said Musk's company built and used gas-burning turbines for power without first obtaining proper permits, and without installing required pollution controls.
In the court's order, published Tuesday , a judge wrote there was "no 'fairly possible' interpretation of the Clean Air Act that would give the United States the right to unilaterally dismiss a citizen suit."
Musk said the boards at Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to discuss a potential merger "at the request of shareholders," noting that these groups "consist of independent directors."
Because Musk is a "conflicted party," he said he can't be in the discussions.

Musk previously pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and President Donald Trump, writing on X that, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government."

Of its $19.6 billion in capital expenditures in the quarter, more than $16.4 billion was committed to the AI business.

Liberal Americans who fled to Europe after President Donald Trump 's re-election shared how the grass is not always greener on the other side of the Atlantic Ocean.
Wired Magazine released an article Thursday headlined "They Fled Trump’s America. Now They Regret It," speaking directly to those who sought "political refuge in the wake of Trump’s second term," but have since voiced frustration with Europe’s lower quality of life, the rise of right-wing politics in those countries, and a newfound appreciation for the cultural norms and niceties of American life.
One account, from a woman nicknamed "Annie," said she was sold the idea of an idyllic U.K. life on social media, "But the reality of life in the U.K. was dramatically different to what she’d imagined ."
"There are huge misconceptions about access to quality healthcare, standard of living… the quality of life is significantly lower than in the U.S.," she told the magazine, citing challenges ranging from their healthcare system to a significantly lower disposable income. "Things in the U.K. that are considered luxury items are very common" in America, like a dishwasher and dryer, she told Wired.

Many expats noted that they grew to appreciate American values and culture after they tried living in Europe. (iStock)
Annie told the outlet that despite believing she'd have free healthcare under the NHS, she now pays "huge amounts of taxes and an immigration surcharge" to access the national healthcare services.
"So no, the health care is not free here," she said.
Annie was also surprised by the amount of anti-American hostility she experienced and cultural differences in the workplace.
"I found it particularly surprising how people feel so comfortable mocking my accent and culture, even in a workplace environment," she said. "The U.K. is very much a place of ‘it is what it is,’ but as Americans we are taught to always improve and strive for better things."
"I thought that ‘British politeness’ existed as it does in movies," Annie added, "but unfortunately, the reality is that present-day British culture is very individualistic, as well as without the sense of charity and helpfulness that many parts of American culture value."
WORLD CUP SOCCER FANS ARE DISCOVERING AMERICA’S GREATNESS. IT’S TIME AMERICANS DID, TOO

Sarah Wood González, a journalist and consultant, made similar comments about learning to appreciate the American mindset and work culture once she was in a different environment.
"Something I had taken for granted is the American outgoingness and default to action, where the question is ‘how can we collaborate?’" she said. "Generally speaking, I also found that the American work style, for better or for worse, moves much faster and can get to a yes or no in less time."
"Finding work was so hard, and the endless bureaucracy had grown worse since I’d left," Josh, who moved to Germany, told Wired. "I missed the friendlier people, freedom of speech, and ease of daily life" in the United States, he said. He added of German daily life, "If you aren’t born and raised there, and don’t look German, you’ll never be fully accepted."
Josh told the magazine he moved back to the U.S. recently and is much happier. He admitted he may have "overreacted" by fleeing to Europe.
Many Americans who shared their regrets on social media were berated by fellow liberals for wanting to move back to "evil" America, the article also said.
"These posts are usually met with a huge amount of backlash. Commenters are quick to imply that the poster must be right-wing and privileged, in for a nasty shock if they did return home," Wired Magazine summarized. "Ironically, many times, they parrot the right-wing notion that they probably aren’t trying hard enough to assimilate into their new country. When one person recently said they badly missed their community of friends in a 'blue city in a blue state' and were considering moving back, the majority of top comments agreed the user was 'insane.'"

Daniel Di Martino, a Manhattan Institute fellow and economist who was born in Venezuela, spoke to Fox News Digital about how some misguided Americans tend to have unrealistic notions about European life.
"Things aren’t always great in Europe, but Europe is not one thing. Living in Greece, making the average salary of a Greek person, would be considered near poverty level in America. Living in Denmark, like an average Dane, is definitely fine, but they still earn much less than the average American," he said. "Some aspects of quality of life in European countries are definitely better: Lower crime, better food. But on the basic reality of how much someone earns, Americans would be worse off moving to Europe."
He concluded, "The reason for this is simple: It is very hard to fire workers, so getting a job in the first place is difficult. And in most European countries other than Switzerland and the Baltics, taxes are very high for low and middle-income workers to pay for so-called universal healthcare and pensions for a larger elderly population."

"American liberals want to import European socialist ideas and wave after wave of third world immigrants into the U.S., but it turns out that in real life, socialism and mass immigration produce countries that are poorer, less productive, and less enjoyable to call home," he said. articles.title_orig: Nigeria confirms Ebola case as outbreak spreads into western Africa
articles.title_zh: Nigeria confirms Ebola case as outbreak spreads into western Africa
articles.content_orig:
Case in Africa’s most populous country was detected in a woman who had travelled from Uganda
Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the health ministry said.
The woman began showing symptoms on 7 October and was admitted to a hospital in Abuja four days later, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola. It is unclear when she arrived in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country.
The health minister, Muhammad Pate, said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. “We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had,” he said.
Uganda’s ministry of health said the patient had only transited through Uganda and that she is a Nigerian woman who had been on a business trip to Congo’s eastern region. The Nigerian authorities have not disclosed her nationality.
“Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said in a statement. The ministry insisted Uganda has “no confirmed active Ebola cases”.
Nigeria is the latest country to report an Ebola case as the outbreak spreads across the region. Kenya confirmed its first case earlier this month and has since recorded nine infections. Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases, but it later declared itself free of the virus.
Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control, said on X that “we are facing an extremely serious threat,” with a fatality rate of nearly 50% of cases.
“This Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has already become the most geographically extensive in history, affecting several countries spread across three regions of Africa,” he said.
The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control said two weeks ago it was stepping up surveillance following the detection of Ebola in Kenya and strengthening the country’s preparedness for a potential outbreak.
“These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of health care workers,” the agency said.
Nigeria established an Ebola taskforce in June after the outbreak in Congo in mid-May.
The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has infected more than 9,500 people and killed more than 4,600 people.
The latest Ebola outbreak is the fastest-spreading on record and is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, the 11,000 people killed in West Africa’s regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, WHO has said.

articles.title_orig: Boeing 737 MAX 10 lands long-awaited FAA certification
articles.title_zh: Boeing 737 MAX 10 lands long-awaited FAA certification
articles.content_orig:
Nearly a decade after Boeing unveiled its largest 737 Max jet, the company has cleared a major hurdle in its effort to bring the plane to airlines. The Federal Aviation Administration approved the Max 10 for passenger service Tuesday, ending years of delays.
The 737 Max 10’s certification represents another milestone in Boeing’s efforts to restore its reputation and financial footing after years of safety, quality and production challenges. With production approved, the aircraft can now be sold to domestic and foreign carriers.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the certification followed “extensive safety reviews,” including thousands of hours of test flights, and called it a major win for American manufacturing.
“To think that it took us almost 10 years to get here. We all probably had a little less gray hair 10 years ago," Duffy said during a visit to Boeing's manufacturing plant Tuesday in Everett, Washington.
The Max 10 is an important piece of the company's effort to regain ground in the narrow-body market. For airlines, the larger plane offers a way to carry more passengers on a single flight, potentially lowering costs per seat. For travelers, it could eventually mean more seats on popular routes, though the impact on fares will depend on how airlines deploy the planes and how much competition they face.
Stephanie Pope, president and CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes, said during Duffy's visit that the certification "clears the path to deliver an airplane that will set a new standard in commercial aviation." The Max 10 will typically seat 185-210 passengers, according to Boeing, compared with 175-195 on the Max 9 and 160-180 on the Max 8.
“Today is a very, very special day. It caps years of hard work and dedication by many," Pope said. "It marks another major milestone in our recovery, and it unlocks a key to our future growth.”
The company expects to begin deliveries in 2027.
The single-aisle jet was introduced at the Paris air show in 2017 to help Boeing compete with rival Airbus. But technical and regulatory hurdles repeatedly delayed certification.
Boeing’s struggles have been particularly acute since two deadly crashes involving the smaller Max 8 killed 346 people in 2018 and 2019 off the coast of Indonesia and in Ethiopia. In 2024, a panel flew off of an Alaska Airlines Max 9 in midair, renewing scrutiny of Boeing’s manufacturing and safety practices.
The delays have held up a key part of Boeing's business. More than 30 customers worldwide have ordered 1,555 Max 10s that Boeing has yet to deliver, accounting for more than 30% of its total 737 Max backlog.
Major customers include United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, American Airlines and Ryanair. Alaska Airlines joined that list in January, ordering 105 Max 10s, with options for 35 more.
The Max 10 is intended to compete with Airbus’s A321neo model family, which entered service in 2017. The largest A321neo can carry more passengers and fly farther without refueling than the Max 10.
Still, Boeing designed the Max 10 to carry more passengers while burning less fuel than older aircraft — a potentially attractive combination for airlines facing soaring jet fuel costs amid the U.S. war with Iran. Those rising costs have put added pressure on airlines to control expenses.
Certification means the FAA has determined that the Max 10’s design meets safety standards, following engineering reviews and flight testing. But Boeing must continue to show it can consistently build the aircraft to the approved design, and each plane must be cleared before it can fly passengers.
The Max 10’s certification completes the lineup of four 737 Max models. The FAA cleared the Max 7 for airline operations in August.
Pope on Tuesday described the certification of both the Max 7 and Max 10 in the same year as a sign of the company’s resilience.
In the wake of the fatal Max 8 crashes, the FAA overhauled how it certifies Boeing aircraft. But over the past 18 months, the agency has gradually eased some of its restrictions on the company, increasing the limit on how many planes Boeing can produce. In July, the FAA also said Boeing could once again issue airworthiness certificates for its 737 Max and 787 planes at the end of production, allowing the company to take back some responsibility for determining whether finished aircraft are ready to fly.

articles.title_zh: Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed?
articles.content_orig:
Kenya is grappling with its first ever outbreak of Ebola, a disease which neighbouring countries, such as Uganda and Democratic Republic of Congo, are used to dealing with.
Nine cases have now been confirmed including its first patient, who travelled from DR Congo and died two weeks ago.
Four relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner have now tested positive, meaning they are all linked to him.
But concerns are rising that the virus could start spreading further, even as the government has sought to assure citizens.
The US has warned it citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert.
Kenyans have been expressing their concerns that the disease could spread more widely.
More than 4,000 people have died since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.
With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread.
The latest outbreak has been caused by the Bundibugyo species, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
Kenyans raised questions from the outset, about how the first patient was able to spend time in the region worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified . He died days after his arrival in Kenya.
As a regional transport hub, the risk of the outbreak spreading is a big concern.
The doctors' union in Kenya has expressed concerns at "lapses" at various border points, including with neighbouring Uganda and Tanzania, as well as at Kenya's main airport.
Dennis Miskellah, the union representative, told the BBC that border and port facilities were grossly understaffed.
However, Health Director-General Patrick Amoth on Tuesday evening sought to reassure people, saying that the eight patients were all improving and responding well to treatment.
When the first case was announced, the authorities urged people not to panic, assuring them of heightened surveillance at airports and border crossings.
Kenya has since introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from 10 countries it considers to be at high risk: DR Congo, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival.
Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases.
Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital.
It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people.
The government has additionally designated treatment and isolation facilities across the country, and health workers have been trained to deal with the disease.
Amoth also said that a dedicated laboratory had been set up at the Kenyatta National Hospital Infectious Disease Unit to handle Ebola tests, to ensure that the hospital's laboratory was not contaminated.
In Kenya, 134 out of 135 people listed as contacts of the first patient remain in quarantine. That means about 99% of the contacts have been traced and isolated, in order to prevent Ebola from spreading to the wider population.
That all of those infected so far had links to the first victim shows Kenya's early response is working, according to the International Rescue Committee.
The government is also working with international partners, including Africa CDC and the World Health Organization (WHO), to support its response, including surveillance, communication and community engagement.
A toll-free emergency hotline, 719, has been provided to the public to report suspected symptoms.
Amoth said that none of the contacts of the first patients had showed symptoms before going into quarantine "and therefore the potential to spread to another person is very minimal, literally non-existent".
The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks. The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
Despite that, Kenya's health ministry says nearly 5,000 healthcare workers have been trained to deal with Ebola at the national and local levels, besides the facilities that have been designated to handle the virus.
The ministry has urged people to remain calm and vigilant. It has also asked Kenyans not to stigmatise people identified as contacts of Ebola cases.
The ministry, along with the WHO, have produced posters to help people understand Ebola and support its containment. One message reads: "Stop stigma, choose support. Stigma can discourage people from reporting symptoms or cooperating with response teams."
In addition, the government has procured supplies of protective equipment.
Not according to the Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Union (KMPDU).
With three health workers and a hospital cleaner among those infected, questions have been asked as to whether the government could do more to protect workers.
Health workers and carers can face a higher risk of Ebola infection because caring for infected patients may bring them into contact with blood and other bodily fluids.
Dennis Miskellah, the KMPDU deputy secretary general, told the BBC that protective equipment must be provided to hospitals so that they are fully protected, especially in case patients with symptoms do not declare that they have been in areas with Ebola.
He suggests the government ought to conduct proper health education to destigmatise the virus, so that people do not seek to hide their symptoms.
The International Rescue Committee has also called for continued funding for contact tracing, border screening and training of frontline health workers in Kenya.
Kenya remains open with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings.
Despite confirming the eight cases, the authorities have explicitly ruled out a national lockdown or general travel ban for Kenyans.
The US on Monday issued an advisory asking citizens to reconsider travelling to the country over Ebola concerns. Other countries have issued health alerts, including the UK, which warned its citizens that they may encounter enhanced health screening, and Canada, which has asked citizens to monitor their health for 21 days.
No country has issued an outright ban against their nationals visiting Kenya, nor have Kenyans been blocked from entering other countries over Ebola fears.
Analysts have raised concerns over the potential impact of public health fears on international travel and tourism but there is no evidence this has happened yet.
But the situation could change if the outbreak were to spread into the wider population.
The exact number of Kenyans living in the DR Congo is not clear.
A report authored last year by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) think-tank put the number of Kenyans living in eastern DR Congo at about 2,500, including about 50 investors. It also noted that there were about four times as many Congolese living in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, alone.
The Kenyan embassy in the Congolese capital, Kinshasa, which represents Kenya's interests in four countries - DR Congo, Central African Republic, Congo-Brazzaville and Gabon - has in the past urged Kenyans living in the region to formally register so that it is able to serve them better.

articles.title_zh: Robert Kabera, Rwandan Government Critic, Beheaded in Uganda
articles.content_orig:
A former Rwandan army sergeant major, who became an outspoken critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded in neighbouring Uganda.
Robert Kabera, 50, fled Rwanda after being accused of sexual assault, which he denied. He sought asylum in neighbouring Uganda, citing political persecution.
Ugandan police spokesperson Kituuma Rusoke on Monday said that Kabera's head had still not been recovered. His body was discovered by local residents on the outskirts of Kampala over the weekend.
The Rwandan government has not publicly commented on the killing. Several critics of Kagame have been killed, both in Rwanda and abroad.
His widow, Jeanne d'Arc Rwigema Uwizeye, told BBC Great Lakes in a written message that she now feared for her family's safety.
"It is scary. I feel crazy, the children and I don't have security," she said.
According to his family, Kabera had travelled to inspect a construction site about 45 km (30 miles) outside Kampala before his death.
Kabera built a public profile as a musician and YouTuber, attracting more than 144,000 subscribers to his channel, which featured over 800 videos, many criticising Kagame and his administration.
Reacting to news of his murder, exiled opposition group Rwanda National Congress (RNC) called for a thorough investigation and for those responsible to be brought to justice.
In a statement on X, the RNC said: "Today, his family is grieving, his voice is gone, and Rwandans in exile are confronting a terrifying question: where can we be safe?"
His death adds to concerns about the safety of Rwandan dissidents living in exile.
In 2014, Patrick Karegeya, a former Rwandan intelligence chief who helped set up the RNC, was found dead in his hotel room in Johannesburg, South Africa.
Karegeya fell out with President Paul Kagame and was arrested twice, serving an 18-month prison sentence for insubordination and desertion before fleeing to South Africa in 2007, where he became a vocal critic of the government.
Following his death, Kagame made remarks widely seen as a warning to other critics.
"Any person alive who may be plotting against Rwanda, whoever they are, will pay the price. Whoever it is, it is a matter of time," he said.
In 2019, South African authorities issued arrest warrants for two Rwandans accused of murdering Karegeya.

The following article by Zhuo Mingliang, Associate Research Fellow at the Academy of Marxism of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences (CASS), examines the work of the Xi Jinping Thought Study Group, set up in 2020 by the London-based Institute for Independence Studies . Among its founders is our co-editor Keith Bennett.
Zhuo introduces the Study Group and its core members, and summarises the main arguments of its 2023 book of memoirs by long-standing friends of China. These include the view that China’s achievements demonstrate the superiority of socialism, and that Xi Jinping Thought is “a great gift to all humanity” that can help unite progressive forces worldwide. He also outlines the Institute’s distinctive positions, among them its emphasis on the non-Western development of scientific socialism and its critique of Western leftists who remain sceptical of socialism with Chinese characteristics.
The article offers an interesting insight into how Chinese scholars view the work of China’s friends in the West – and into the role of people-to-people movements in breaking through the anti-China consensus in the Western media.
The article was originally published in Chinese in the Journal of Handan University (Vol. 36, No. 3, September 2026). The English translation is by Friends of Socialist China; quotations from Keith Bennett’s preface are translated back from the Chinese and will not match his original wording.
Abstract: The “Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era Study Group” is an academic research organisation set up by left-wing British scholars who know China well and are friendly towards it. Writing from the standpoint of overseas people with first-hand experience, its members affirm the international influence of Xi Jinping Thought. They recognise the superiority of the socialist system as shown by China’s development path, and they rebut false anti-China narratives in the West.
Western non-governmental groups that know China and are friendly to it are an important force for breaking down US and Western media bias against China. The article therefore recommends four lines of work:
The aim is to use civil-society forces to “tell China’s story well”, grow a friendly international climate of opinion towards China, and strengthen the popular basis for people-to-people ties between China and other countries.
Keywords: Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era; Britain’s Institute for Independence Studies; scientific socialism
At present, British people who know and are friendly towards China follow China’s achievements in reform and development closely. They actively study Xi Jinping Thought, Chinese modernisation, China’s global initiatives and “Chinese solutions”. In doing so they have helped improve mutual understanding between the Chinese and British peoples and helped the international community see China objectively and fairly.
One of these is the “Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era Study Group”. It is an important academic body under the Institute for Independence Studies, and it works to study and spread Xi Jinping Thought in Britain and around the world. It has published a book, Paths to Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics for a New Era: Memoirs of Long-Standing Friends of China and Solidarity Activists . Its views and positions deserve our close attention.
The Institute for Independence Studies is an independent body based in London, founded by left-wing scholars from several countries. It is dedicated to researching and spreading the ideas of social and national liberation, and to applying them to social reality in the era of imperialism. This work is carried out especially through the writings and activities of Keith Bennett.
In August 2020 the Institute set up the Study Group. Its purpose is to study and spread Xi Jinping Thought, to draw from it experience of universal significance for understanding the new era, and to promote the flourishing of intellectual, academic and cultural life in its own country. Its core members include:
The Study Group’s first major undertaking after its founding was to edit and publish Paths to Xi Jinping Thought: Memoirs of Long-Standing Friends of China and Solidarity Activists . Published in 2023, it is a collection of memoirs by international friends and senior figures in friendship organisations who have long worked for friendship with China and firmly supported its development.
The authors draw on their own experience to review their history of engagement with China. They bear vivid witness to China’s leap forward in the new era. On that basis they explain how they understand and identify with the formation of Xi Jinping Thought and its practical power.
The book offers the distinctive observations of overseas eyewitnesses, stepping outside the usual perspectives of domestic research. It shows the far-reaching influence of Xi Jinping Thought in three areas: guiding China’s development, promoting friendship and mutual trust between China and other countries, and helping to build a community with a shared future for mankind. It also shows how this thought is being spread and recognised ever more widely in the international community.
In the book’s Preface, Keith Bennett writes:
“Today the socialist countries are the collective leading force of the international working class and progressive movement. In terms of global reach and explanatory power, Xi Jinping Thought is the most influential body of thought among these countries. British socialists, like their comrades around the world, should therefore find effective ways to guide progressive people to study and deeply understand this valuable intellectual resource. Accomplishing this task means confronting many unresolved questions. We have long felt that how to make revolution in Western Europe remains an unanswered question, and for decades since we have been searching for the answer.” [1]
Bennett regards the book as an important contribution to that search. It collects the personal experiences and reflections of some long-standing friends of China. Over several decades these people have followed varied and complex political and intellectual paths, yet each in their own way confirms that “Xi Jinping Thought has universal applicability to the great task of uniting socialists and other progressive people and arming them ideologically.” [2]
Compiling the book took hundreds of hours of collaborative work. This included in-person meetings, in-depth interviews and thematic seminars, as well as telephone and online meetings during the Covid-19 pandemic. The process produced a large body of recordings and transcripts, which give a solid basis for further research. The main pieces in the book include “China Under Xi Jinping and the Anti-Imperialist Struggle of Our Time” and “China in the Xi Jinping Era and Communism”. Its main views are as follows:
(1) China now stands at the centre of the world stage. That reality alone should be reason enough for anyone who wants to understand the world rationally to study Xi Jinping Thought in depth. (2) Xi Jinping Thought is the guiding thought created and summed up by the Communist Party of China and its leaders. It has led China to great transformation and great achievements. Elon Musk-led SpaceX issued its second-ever quarterly earnings report.
Elon Musk-led aerospace giant SpaceX grew revenue by 161% over three months ending in September compared with the same period a year earlier, according to an earnings release issued on Tuesday.
The surge in revenue was owed in large part to a significant expansion of the company's businesses centered on artificial intelligence and Starlink, a satellite internet service, the earnings showed.
SpaceX said it earned overall profit of $4.40 billion in its most recent quarter, turning around from a loss of $1.05 billion in the same three-month period a year earlier.
The company also recorded a loss in the previous quarter ending in June, meaning the latest earnings report marked a turn into profitability.
Shares of SpaceX jumped nearly 4% in after-hours trading after the earnings release, putting the price of a share at about $153.30.
The company, which Musk helms as founder and CEO, boasts a valuation of nearly $1.95 trillion. The earnings amounted to the company's second-ever quarterly financial disclosure since it went public in June.
In its first earnings release, in August, SpaceX said it generated $7.8 billion in revenue over three months ending in June. That figure marked an increase from $4 billion in revenue over the same period a year earlier, but the revenue failed to keep up with costs.
SpaceX builds and operates spacecraft, including thousands of satellites deployed in support of its Starlink satellite internet service. The company also oversees xAI, which offers a chatbot in competition with the likes of OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude.
Starlink, the main driver of the company’s profits, received attention from investors ahead of the release.
Earlier this month, Starlink acquired nationwide, low-band spectrum, suggesting the company will seek to compete with U.S. mobile carriers, Paul Golding, senior digital infrastructure and payments analyst at Macquarie, said in a statement to ABC News.
"We'll be listening for launch timing, terrestrial build plans and appetite for more spectrum," Golding said.
On Tuesday, SpaceX announced $5.2 billion in revenue over the most recent quarter from its connectivity segment, which includes Starlink. That figure indicates a rise of 69% from the same quarter a year earlier, earnings showed.
SpaceX has spent significantly on efforts to develop AI infrastructure, such as data centers. Last quarter, the company's AI unit recorded an operating loss of $1.26 billion, in part because AI spending more than doubled from the previous quarter.
The AI unit turned positive over three months ending in September, however, registering $431 million in income from operations.
The earnings release arrived a day after Musk vowed to give every child in the United States a share of stock in aerospace giant SpaceX.
"Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many," Musk said in a post on X .
The latest U.S. Census data estimated about 73 million people in the U.S. under age 18. Using that figure and given the company's share price of about $150 on the day of Musk's announcement, the giveaway would total nearly $11 billion. As of Tuesday afternoon, the share price has fallen slightly to about $148 a share.
Musk's net worth stands at $927.4 billion, the most recent Fortune data shows, meaning the donation would amount to about 1.1% of his wealth.
The pledge from Musk came amid scrutiny from some policymakers, investors and the general public about the potential impact of AI on the labor market and wider economy.
A surge in AI spending has helped boost the U.S. economy in recent quarters, but some economists have warned the industry may increase inflation and harm job prospects for some workers.
A series of autonomous AI hacks in recent months, meanwhile, has elicited concern from some industry insiders and public figures about severe risks the technology could pose for key institutions with digital systems
Analysts who previously spoke to ABC News disagreed sharply about the likelihood of an AI-induced calamity. Some said such an outcome is likely if the industry fails to impose adequate safeguards, while others characterized it as vague and far-fetched.

Microsoft's next-gen Xbox hardware lineup is beginning to come into focus. According to a new report from Fortune , the company is gearing up to ship new hardware in the form of a handheld in 2027, followed by a full-blown console in 2028.
It's unclear if the handheld project is a first party Xbox device, or a third-party device designed and manufactured by an OEM partner like ASUS and the ROG Ally X . The console is expected to be first-party, and is likely to run a specialized version of Windows.
The report claims that Xbox and Windows have been at odds about how the OS should run on Project Helix. Windows leaders wanted the consoles to run a modified version of Windows desktop, but Xbox leaders wanted a more boutique OS experience designed for gaming.
"Tensions ran high enough that a senior Xbox executive threatened to scrap the handheld project rather than adopt the Windows build ... Xbox is now largely controlling the direction of the operating system for the project" Fortune claims.
Windows already powers the current Xbox Series consoles, as well as Xbox One. It's a modified version of the OS that the Xbox team has customized, built on top of the Windows OS core that is developed by the Windows team. It sounds like the Xbox team has decided to maintain this approach with Project Helix consoles.
Alarmingly, Fortune claims that Microsoft is currently expecting the next-gen Xbox console to cost somewhere between $1,200 and $1,800, making it the most expensive gaming console ever. articles.title_zh: Microsoft reportedly projects $1,200 to $1,800 price for 2028 Project Helix
articles.content_orig:
We haven’t heard many details about Microsoft’s upcoming “Project Helix” gaming hardware since the company announced it in March as a device that will “play your Xbox and PC games.” In a new wide-ranging profile of Xbox CEO Asha Sharma , though, Fortune alludes to a dual release strategy for upcoming Microsoft gaming hardware, with “a next-generation handheld device” planned by the end of next year and a 2028 holiday season console release that could cost between $1,200 and $1,800.
That future console price range is based on what has “internally been projected” at the company, according to Fortune. But the price for consumers could come down if “Microsoft decides to subsidize the cost,” the outlet says, as many console makers have done in the past .
While a $1,200 starting price would be historically high for the game console market, even accounting for inflation , it also reflects a new normal: The slowdown in Moore’s Law and AI-driven component shortages mean cutting-edge gaming hardware just isn’t as cheap as it used to be. This year, the Steam Machine broke the $1,000 starting price , while the 2-year-old technology in the PlayStation 5 Pro is now going for $900 , and the 6-year-old Xbox Series X now starts at $750 .
Fortune also reports that Microsoft is beset by internal clashes over whether its upcoming Helix handheld will run a “trimmed-down version of Windows Home”—akin to last year’s ROG Xbox Ally —or a bespoke operating system built and controlled by the Xbox group. Fortune cites “people briefed on the clash” in reporting that one high-level executive threatened to cancel the handheld altogether if they were forced to use Windows.
That threat seemingly helped lead to the current situation with the Xbox team “now largely controlling the direction of the operating system for the project, Fortune writes, though Sharma said the two groups are still working closely together. Fortune also reports that Microsoft has pressured the hardware team to move up the timelines for Project Helix hardware “by at least several months,” in part by using AI tools where applicable.
The profile also cites “people familiar with the strategy” in reporting that Xbox Game Pass will soon shift to a heavily tiered “a la carte” structure that lets subscribers pick and choose “add-ons for console-only games, cloud gaming, and multiplayer.” That would be an interesting shift from the current Game Pass plans, which all include some level of cloud-based gaming, console exclusives, and console multiplayer even for players who don’t make use of them.
Elsewhere in the wide-ranging profile, Fortune addresses concerns from “several current and former staff members” that Sharma was put in place merely to enact painful cuts before an impending sale of a spinoff of the Xbox group. But the piece also quotes Microsoft executive Judson Althoff pushing back against that idea, saying, “We would not have put [Sharma] on a business we intend to sell. There’s going to be a ton of speculation about all this. Time will tell.”

articles.title_orig: Utah sues Kalshi, saying it’s ‘the manager of a back-alley gambling den’
articles.title_zh: Utah sues Kalshi, saying it’s ‘the manager of a back-alley gambling den’
articles.content_orig:
Utah filed a lawsuit Tuesday against Kalshi, arguing the prediction market platform is subject to the state’s anti-gambling laws.
Along with the lawsuit, Attorney General Derek Brown declared gambling a “public nuisance” in Utah that causes harm to its residents.
Utah — one of two states that prohibit all forms of gambling — is the latest state to challenge a prediction market company in court. At least nine states have brought legal actions against prediction market platforms. While most are civil lawsuits, at least one state, Arizona, filed a criminal complaint.
The 63-page Utah lawsuit filed in 3rd District Court in Salt Lake City seeks to stop the company from operating in the state, as well as collect millions of dollars in damages.
“Under Utah law, I have determined that this operation is causing a significant and substantial ongoing harm to a significant number of Utahns,” Brown said at a news conference.
“And so today we are asking the court to stop sports, elections, politics, culture and mention bets here in Utah, and to use a court-approved geolocation provider to enforce this. We’re also asking the court to make the defendants give up the profits that they have made to pay restitution and to be accountable for the public nuisance that they have caused here in the state of Utah.”
Kalshi issued a statement later Tuesday saying the company is a federally regulated financial exchange, like the stock market. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission oversees prediction markets.
“Our customers trade with each other and set the prices. As a national derivatives market overseen by the CFTC, Kalshi answers to federal law, and no single state should have a veto over it. This latest state court action does not affect our ongoing federal litigation,” said Kalshi spokesperson Jacki McGavick.
The lawsuit seeks to pull back Kalshi’s “illegally obtained profits” in the state. Kalshi takes a one- to two-cent fee for every wager, per the lawsuit. Based on those numbers, the state estimates the company made between $30.5 million and $61.1 million from bets placed by Utah accounts.
But those numbers could change.
“As we get discovery in the course of this civil complaint, we anticipate having more information that will help us understand exactly what it is that they’ve made and how they’ve done it in the course of effectively breaking Utah law,” Brown said.
According to the lawsuit, at least 1.1% of wagers on Kalshi involve Utah accounts, totaling more than 3 billion bet as of Oct. 19, 2026. More than 32,000 Utahns had verified Kalshi accounts as of February 2026, per the lawsuit, but state officials believe the number has grown substantially since then.
Utah bettors lost at least $5.5 million based on reported nationwide retail losses and the state’s share of the activity, according to the suit.
In February, Kalshi sued Utah in federal court to block the state from enforcing its gambling laws against the company. The company argued that because it operates a federally registered exchange, the state could not treat its sports bets as gambling.
The New York-based prediction market allows users to place “event contracts” on future outcomes and earn a payout if they are correct. Those transactions are regulated through the CFTC. Kalshi argued the state planned to prevent the company from offering contracts in Utah and asked the courts to block any enforcement that “interferes with the operation and function of plaintiffs’ futures market.”
Utah joined 40 states and the District of Columbia earlier this year in a letter to the CFTC contending the commission does not have jurisdiction over sports betting. The states argue that sports betting on prediction markets through “event contracts” is indistinguishable from traditional sports betting. The CFTC has historically monitored futures contracts on things such as livestock, crude oil and gold and silver prices.
In August, U.S. District Judge Robert J. Shelby ruled that Utah’s anti-gambling laws apply to sports betting contracts Kalshi offers on its platform. He concluded that the federal law Kalshi relied upon in the case does not preempt the state’s ability to enforce its statutes.
That ruling factored into Utah’s decision to sue Kalshi in state court.
“Although the defendants are well aware that sports bets and other forms of gambling are illegal under Utah law, defendants chose to begin offering gambling bets to Utah’s residents by at least September 2024, something they continue to doing despite a a recent federal court order rejecting KalshiEx’s argument that it is not bound by Utah law,” according to the lawsuit.
The lawsuit contends Kalshi advertises its platform as “legal in all 50 states,” including ads that aired in Utah. It also alleges that a Kalshi representative filmed an ad on the campus of Brigham Young University, a private university sponsored by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.
Earlier this month, a member of the faith’s First Presidency condemned gambling, including prediction markets, in a speech during the church’s general conference.
“For us as Latter-day Saints, overarching all other concerns is the fact that gambling is morally wrong,” said President D. Todd Christofferson, second counselor in the First Presidency. “Gambling is built on the desire to obtain something for nothing. Its structure requires that any gain comes at others’ expense. It’s hard to reconcile that with the commandment to love our neighbor as ourselves.”
Brown said in the news conference that prediction markets do not help people invest. “Frankly, they are engineered to do one thing and one thing alone, and that is to empty your wallet,” he said.
In addition to Kalshi, the lawsuit names related entities KalshiEx, Kalshi Klear, Kalshi Trading, Susquehanna International Group and Susquehanna Government Products as defendants.
