articles.title_orig: PHP warns admins of two critical flaws, emergency patches coming tomorrow
articles.title_zh: PHP warns admins of two critical flaws, emergency patches coming tomorrow
articles.content_orig:
Details of CVE-2926-109618 and CVE-2926-109619 leak ahead of official update as analysts warn vulns should be taken “seriously”.
The PHP security team warned users of an upcoming Critical PHP Security Release in a brief post on October 20 regarding “two critical vulnerabilities, both rated CVSS v4.0 9.2”.
“All PHP users are encouraged to prepare now so they can upgrade as soon as the release is available,” PHP said .
“We reserve the right to release earlier should details of either vulnerability become public, or should evidence of active exploitation appear in the wild.”
The advisory added that full details, which versions are impacted, and which versions were fixed would be published alongside the release; however, it appears details have already leaked – and the vulnerabilities look serious.
PVP had already said both vulnerabilities featured CVSS scores of 9.2, which is bad enough. They are both, however, also remote code execution vulnerabilities and, according to cyber security firm watchTowr, very real and very worrying.
“Information has leaked wrt zero-day embargoed RCE vulns in PHP. We can confirm that they're real. CVE-2926-109618/619,” the company said in an overnight post to X .
“We cannot share further information right now. Take this seriously and apply patches when available.”
Benjamin Harris, the company’s CEO, shared information on the developments with Cyber Daily.
"In the last hour, two remote code execution vulnerabilities in PHP have been leaked. These vulnerabilities were previously scheduled under embargo and due for release on Thursday at 11 am ET,” Harris said overnight. “While we are not able to share technical information at this point for obvious reasons, given the sensitivity, we can confirm that these vulnerabilities are indeed real.”
However, while PHP had originally said the vulnerabilities were less than a perfect 10, watchTowr has said that is exactly what they are, and that they impact PHP versions 5, 6, 7, and 8. “Patches are currently unavailable, but we anticipate that the patch release will now be significantly faster and swifter than the Thursday at 11 am that was previously scheduled,” Harris added.
watchTowr said it has already successfully reproduced CVE-2026-109618; the company added it “will wait for the patches from PHP before sharing any further information”.
PHP is an open-source scripting language designed primarily for web development.

King Charles III praised Oman's peacemaking attempts in the Middle East Tuesday as Sultan Haitham bin Tariq began the first state visit by an Omani ruler to the U.K. in nearly half a century.
Hailing longstanding diplomatic, military and royal ties at a Windsor Castle banquet, the British monarch paid tribute to Muscat's "noble efforts" to help reopen the choked Strait of Hormuz.
"I would especially like to recognize, at a time when conflict has returned so painfully to the region, Oman's enduring commitment as a trusted interlocutor to all parties," Charles told around 160 guests at the lavish dinner.
"Oman's role across the Gulf and her 'constructive neutrality' — as you put it — matters far beyond Hormuz, and is worthy of our utmost respect," Britain's king added in a toast to the Omani sultan.
The first state visit to Britain by a sultan of Oman for 44 years comes amid severe turbulence in the Middle East prompted by the U.S.-Iran war.
Oman, a key U.K. military ally which borders the vital Hormuz waterway, has acted as a mediator in talks between the U.S. and Iran since the conflict flared in late February.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth confirmed Tuesday that he visited Israel on Monday and met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, saying he "was there visiting our troops" and "had a chance to talk to the prime minister."
The unannounced visit came just over a week before Netanyahu's party faces elections. It also comes after President Trump floated resuming military operations against Iran following next month's U.S. midterm elections.
"Of course, the nature of our conversations is not something I would talk about but they've been good partners and I appreciate that," Hegseth said of his meeting with Netanyahu.
U.S. diplomatic missions across the Middle East have issued a new round of security warnings to Americans amid escalating attacks by Iran-backed Houthi militants against Saudi Arabia, including an Oct. 10 strike on Riyadh's international airport that killed an American citizen.
The alerts, issued Sunday by U.S. embassies in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and several other countries, warned that hostilities could rapidly and without warning spread beyond areas already affected by the fighting. The advisories urged Americans to exercise vigilance and prepare for possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions.
"We are actively warning U.S. citizens about the very real threat the Houthis pose and urging them to heed official guidance," Edgar Vasquez, the State Department's deputy assistant secretary for press, told CBS News.
"These alerts are part of a proactive effort by the Trump administration to ensure Americans are aware of potential risks," Vasquez said, adding that the safety and security of American citizens remain the department's "top priority."
President Trump said the U.S. is "doing very well with Iran" and he's just deciding how he wants to win the war.
"As you know, we're doing very well with Iran," Mr. Trump said as he took questions from reporters in the Oval Office at an unrelated executive order signing. "We just have to make a final decision of which way do we want to win? Do we want to win the nice way or the not nice way? But we're doing very well."
The war, which Mr. Trump said would take only a few weeks in March, has now dragged on for almost eight months with no apparent end in sight. Iran said on Tuesday it would not return to the negotiating table unless the U.S. drops its sanctions, threats and pressure campaign — an unlikely demand.
The president also discussed Europe not helping the U.S. with the war with Iran, saying, "We don't need any help. But I was testing them."
"I just called individual presidents and prime ministers to ask, would they like to help us? And they said, 'No,'" Mr. Trump said. "I said, 'Well, that's not nice.' You know, we spend hundreds of billions a year on NATO. And they said no."
Iran is taking a hard-line stance on negotiations with the U.S. to end the war, with President Masoud Pezeshkian saying Tuesday there will be no return to talks without a halt to the pressure campaign by the U.S.
Pezeshkian met with representatives from Pakistan, including army chief Asim Munir, on Tuesday. Pakistan has played an integral role as a mediator in peace talks between the U.S. and Iran, including the brief success of the Islamabad Memorandum in June.
"(Pezeshkian) told Pakistan's Field Marshal Asim Munir that US warmongering lies behind regional tensions, including disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz," according to a readout of the meeting from the official Iranian government account on X . "He said Washington must lift its pressures, threats and sanctions before any negotiations."
Those conditions are unlikely to be agreed upon by the U.S., which has stepped up its sanctions , dubbed Operation Economic Outcast, over the past month. President Trump has said the economic pressure campaign has become the main strategy for ending the war.

Iranian forces have, since the outbreak of the Middle East war, repeatedly targeted ships attempting to pass through Hormuz via a southern, U.S.-approved route close to the Omani coast.

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby gave a wide-ranging, often provocative interview to the New York Times, defending fees for aisle and window seats and countering the rise in airfares by asserting "it's expensive to fly airplanes."
"There are customers that pay more that get more," Kirby, 59, said in the interview that ran Oct. 18 .
But he struck a decidedly more populist note on the topic of wealth inequality — which he brought up when the Times asked him about waning trust in CEOs and his responsibility in dispelling it. Here's his full answer:
"Wealth inequality has become a danger to our society, and we need to address that," he said. "We should have a national wealth tax — it won't work by state because people will just move. And I think we should have inheritance taxes that get close to 100% at some level. I would pay them."
United Airlines stock rose 0.3% before the bell on Tuesday.
Kirby is not the first or only business titan to call for bigger taxes on the wealthiest Americans. Luminaries like Warren Buffett, Bill Gates, and George Soros have long advocated for increasing the tax burden at their rarefied wealth levels.
Read more: How much does a millionaire actually owe the IRS on tax day?
"We've updated our tax system before to keep up with changing times, and we need to do it again, starting with raising taxes on people like me," Gates wrote on his blog in 2020.
Marc Benioff, CEO of Salesforce ( CRM ), wrote in 2019 that "increasing taxes on high-income individuals like myself would help generate the trillions of dollars that we desperately need to improve education and healthcare and fight climate change."
Joe Biden was president, and Democrats in Congress were gearing up to pass legislation to tax unrealized gains on individuals with a net worth of at least $1 billion or annual income of $100 million for three consecutive years. Of course, that never happened, and after President Trump was reelected, Republicans in Congress passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which included provisions that made lower marginal tax rates for high incomes permanent, along with other provisions benefiting wealthy Americans.
Read more: 10 ways the One Big Beautiful Bill Act affects student loans and financial aid
As for the inheritance taxes Kirby said he favors, there is no federal tax on individual beneficiaries of inherited assets. A few states impose a state inheritance tax.
There is a federal estate tax, but the exemption is so large — $15 million per person — that few people ever pay it. Only 0.2% of estates are large enough to be subject to the tax, and even then the tax applies only to the amount that exceeds the exemption threshold.

Tesla ( TSLA ) will report third quarter results after the closing bell on Wednesday, with profits and cash flow squarely in focus, with a dash of merger speculation.
Tesla is expected to report Q3 revenue of $28.13 billion, flat year over year, per Bloomberg consensus. Adjusted EPS is estimated at $0.44, with adjusted EBITDA of $3.66 billion.

This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed.
Tesla stock is still down about 17% this year, a test for investors, but typically the company rallies on stronger deliveries in the back half of the year.
Tesla reported Q3 deliveries of 486,532, down 2% from a year ago but well ahead of Bloomberg consensus of 463,000. Energy storage deployments came in at 13.7 GWh, up from 12.5 GWh a year ago and Q2's 13.5 GWh.
Tesla's sales in its key territories are moving in different directions. The US is still feeling the loss of the $7,500 federal EV tax credit, which set off a buying rush in last year's third quarter before it expired. Cox Automotive estimates Tesla sold around 144.1K EVs in the US in Q3, down nearly 20% year over year. That was still about 54% of the US EV market, more than all other brands combined.
Tesla's Shanghai, however, posted a September wholesale volume of 95,366 vehicles, its best month of 2026, with exports up 58%, while domestic sales fell 9%. In Europe, Tesla registrations across the EU, UK, and EFTA rose 43.3% from January through August, per ACEA .
Free cash flow (FCF) is again the number to watch, and it's expected to be deeply negative. Per Tesla's own sell-side analyst consensus , Wall Street sees Q3 FCF at -$4.51 billion, with capital expenditures climbing to $7.77 billion for the quarter. A year ago, FCF was nearly $4 billion.
Tesla has guided to more than $25 billion in capex for 2026, vs. roughly $8.5 billion spent last year. The money is going to Optimus production lines, AI compute, the Cybercab ramp, and the Terafab chip plant it is building with SpaceX.
Elon Musk made clear over the weekend where he thinks that spending pays off. "Optimus and Cybercab will be the vast majority of Tesla's value," Tesla's CEO posted on X on Saturday.
Tesla began commercial Cybercab service in Austin on Sept. 3, but federal regulators have questions. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) issued Tesla a special order with 21 requests on how it self-certified the Cybercab, which has no steering wheel or pedals, as compliant with federal safety standards. Tesla asked for an extension to Nov. 20. NHTSA granted 30 days instead , making answers due Oct. 30.
Tesla also finally revealed its long-delayed Roadster last Thursday at SpaceX's ( SPCX ) facility in Waco, Texas. The car used cold-gas thrusters to jump over several Teslas, including a Semi, and land. Tesla said the Roadster hit 0-60 mph in 0.81 seconds in a test at the event, and Musk said production starts in 2028.
Deepwater's Gene Munster called it an "engineering flex" with little commercial value, and Morningstar expects the Roadster to sell fewer than 2,000 units a year.
Then there's SpaceX. Barclays analyst Dan Levy wrote last week that a Tesla-SpaceX tie-up "has increasingly become the consensus expectation." He pointed to Tesla's annual meeting , expected by Dec. 6, as a possible venue for a shareholder vote. Barclays sees an all-stock deal with SpaceX as the buyer.
Investors shouldn't expect clarity on Wednesday; Musk said in July that discussing a deal wouldn't be appropriate on an earnings call.

The European Union has strongly criticized the eastern Libyan parliament’s ratification on Tuesday of Libya’s maritime memorandum with Turkey, reiterating that the agreement violates the sovereign rights of third countries and does not comply with the Law of the Sea.
The EU stressed that its position, established by the European Council in 2019, remains unchanged, describing the agreement as “invalid and void”. It also reaffirmed its solidarity with Greece and Cyprus and reiterated its opposition to any external intervention in Libya.
In a joint statement, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and the President of the European Council Antonio Costa noted: “We deeply regret the ratification today by the Libyan Parliament of the so-called Libyan-Türkiye Memorandum of Understanding on the delimitation of maritime jurisdictions in the Mediterranean Sea.”
“We recall that the EU’s position on this matter was clearly stated by the European Council in 2019 and remains unchanged,” it said adding:
“This agreement infringes upon the sovereign rights of third states, it does not comply with the Law of the Sea, and is null and void. We reaffirm our solidarity with Greece and Cyprus. We reiterate the EU’s well known position against any outside interference in Libya.”
Libya’s eastern parliament backed the maritime agreement with Turkey on Tuesday, reviving a deal that Athens has long opposed.
Control of Libya ​is split between rival western and eastern administrations, ​with the east under military commander Khalifa Haftar.
The maritime deal covering claims in the eastern Mediterranean had been agreed with Turkey in 2019 by the internationally recognized Government of National Accord (GNA) in ​the west, but ​was rejected by authorities in eastern Libya, sparking a ​boycott, and in Egypt and Greece.

articles.title_orig: Hegseth meets with Netanyahu in Israel ahead of elections and possible restart to Iran war
articles.title_zh: Hegseth meets with Netanyahu in Israel ahead of elections and possible restart to Iran war
articles.content_orig:
Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth quietly visited Israel on Monday and met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, according to a senior U.S. military official who spoke to CBS News under condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
A second source involved in the matter in Israel confirmed Tuesday morning that Netanyahu met Hegseth.
The unannounced visit came just over a week before Netanyahu's party faces elections. It also comes after President Trump floated resuming military operations against Iran following next month's U.S. midterm elections.
Hegseth confirmed the visit in comments to reporters Tuesday, saying he "was there visiting our troops" and "had a chance to talk to the prime minister."
"Of course, the nature of our conversations is not something I would talk about but they've been good partners and I appreciate that," Hegseth said.
The Pentagon declined to comment on the visit. CBS News has reached out to the Israeli government for comment.
Axios was first to report Hegseth's visit.
Israeli and U.S. forces jointly launched strikes against Iran in late February, and the two allies worked closely with each other early in the war. The U.S. also struck three Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025 during a broader conflict between Israel and Iran.
Iran and the U.S. have largely refrained from striking each other in recent weeks, but Mr. Trump has said openly that he is still weighing whether to cut a deal with Iran's leadership or "annihilate" the country — a decision he says could come after the November midterm elections .
Netanyahu, the longest-serving prime minister in Israeli history, faces his own political uncertainty a week from Tuesday. The coalition led by his right-wing Likud party is seeking to remain in power, but it faces several more centrist challengers, including one party run by former Israel Defense Forces chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot.
Netanyahu told Israeli media last week he is not planning to launch renewed strikes against Iran before the Oct. 27 elections, saying , "it is not convenient for us."
Mr. Trump endorsed Netanyahu on Sunday , calling him "a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran."
The U.S. president has maintained a close relationship with Netanyahu, though he has put pressure on Israel at times. Over the spring and summer, the Trump administration urged Israel to ease up on striking Lebanon, home to Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah.
The administration has also encouraged Israel to crack down on settler violence in the West Bank and cut a longer-term deal with Hamas in the Gaza Strip.
Last month, Trump envoy Jared Kushner suggested the upcoming Israeli elections may have delayed progress in Gaza, saying at a conference in Kyiv: "They just have a crazy election, and that makes them a little irrational in certain regards."

articles.title_orig: Gemini's Personal Intelligence is coming to cars
articles.title_zh: Gemini's Personal Intelligence is coming to cars
articles.content_orig:
Google kicked off 2026 with the addition of Personal Intelligence to Gemini, allowing its AI to pull in more of your data to formulate answers. It started as a paid feature but eventually came to all Gemini users. However, this feature wasn’t available in the car until now. Google is rolling out Personal Intelligence to Android Auto and Google Built-in, and it is still, thankfully, an optional feature.
As Google points out , a generative AI’s outputs are better “when it knows the world and knows you,” which is correct in an uncomfortable sort of way. The more context you can provide to a model, the better the output will be at the end of the token shuffle. Since Google has so much of your data already, it sees Personal Intelligence as a differentiator versus other AI systems. You don’t have to provide the AI context because it already has it from apps like Gmail and Calendar.
Personal Intelligence is beginning its rollout in Android Auto today, and it will come to vehicles with Google built-in in the next few months. As an aside, “Google built-in” is questionable branding, but it refers to cars that run Google software in the infotainment system rather than projecting an interface from your phone. Very few vehicles have Google built-in, but Google often releases new car features on them first. This time, it’s the other way around.
Google says Personal Intelligence is a natural fit for the car, allowing you to focus on the road instead of providing detailed instructions to your digital assistant. For example, you can say “take me to my doctor’s appointment,” and Gemini can get that data from your connected calendar. It can also leverage visual analysis to find locations in your photos to begin navigation.
Personal Intelligence is off by default, but it’s possible you’ve turned it on at some point while interacting with Gemini, which has now replaced Assistant on all devices. Google has a habit of nudging users to opt in to data sharing in Gemini, so you may not even realize you’re sharing account data with Gemini, and those settings will transfer over to Android Auto. For Google built-in vehicles, you only get personal results if you’ve connected a device over Bluetooth. You will be able to turn this off via in-car settings even if your phone has Personal Intelligence enabled.
There may be other people interacting with the screen in your car, so perhaps you don’t want more of your account data informing replies. The Personal Intelligence options are just one level deep in the Gemini app’s settings. You’re looking for the “Connected Apps” section, where you can toggle Workspace (Gmail, Calendar, etc.), Search, Photos, and more.
While Google says it doesn’t use your personal data to train Gemini, it does use your inputs and outputs while using the AI. Some of those outputs can have personal information when you have these services connected, and while the company does attempt to filter that out, it won’t make any promises . The rollout of Personal Intelligence in your car is probably a good opportunity to check your data-sharing settings and make sure you’re comfortable with them.

articles.title_orig: China slams US ban on DeepSeek AI over security concerns
articles.title_zh: China slams US ban on DeepSeek AI over security concerns
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration banned Chinese AI startup DeepSeek from civilian U.S. government agencies, citing security concerns.
The Department of Homeland Security on Monday made public the order requiring federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek-related technology from their IT systems and barring them from procuring DeepSeek products and services. The ban applies to federal civilian agency IT systems, including third-party products and services developed using the company's technology.
The move comes amid intensifying geopolitical tensions between Washington and Beijing, with artificial intelligence emerging as a key battleground in the two countries' race for technological dominance.
Asked about the U.S. move by Reuters, China's foreign ministry told the news agency that it would safeguard the rights and interests of its companies.
Mao Ning, a ministry spokesperson, said that "China consistently opposes the over-generalization of national security as well as the politicization of science, technology and trade issues," the agency reported.
The order, originally issued on July 24, applies to federal civilian agencies, including the Treasury, State and Justice departments, but it excludes the Department of Defense.
Since DeepSeek burst onto the scene at the start of 2025, several U.S. government agencies have imposed various restrictions.
Congress restricted the use of DeepSeek in intelligence community systems in December 2025. Earlier that year in March, U.S. Commerce Department bureaus told staff DeepSeek was banned on government devices, Reuters reported at the time. The Defense Information Systems Agency moved to block access to DeepSeek models in January 2025, according to reports from Bloomberg.
DeepSeek's AI models "present multiple threat vectors," the latest DHS order states, citing concerns over potential access to sensitive data by Chinese authorities and potential cybersecurity vulnerabilities.
The agency also warned that using DeepSeek's AI models could result in sensitive U.S. government data being transferred to China, potentially providing intelligence on American citizens and government programs.
The models may also contain malware or other security vulnerabilities, the agency said, citing open-source research that identified multiple critical vulnerabilities in DeepSeek's iOS app.
Executive agencies can request exceptions to the order, including delays in compliance, by submitting a written justification to the DHS within 60 days of the order's issuance.
DeepSeek and China's Embassy in the U.K. did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

Surprise! Hot on the heels of PlayStation's own upscaling tech announcements, Microsoft and AMD just revealed that the firm's flagship FSR 4.1 tech is coming to the Xbox platform.
FSR (FidelityFX Super Resolution) is a technology from AMD that renders games at a lower resolution, and then uses machine learning to generate a sharper image. Since the hardware isn't working as hard, that overhead can be used for performance.
FSR 4.1 is a big leap over previous versions, and Microsoft has partnered with AMD to bring it not only to Xbox Series X , but also Xbox Ally X , Xbox Ally S and Xbox Series S — the latter two of which should benefit from very, very big performance boosts as a result.
"At Xbox, we're building a gaming platform designed to meet players where they are, and make it easier for creators to reach them," Xbox CTO Scott Van Vilet explained. "AMD has been an important partner in that journey for more than two decades. Together our teams have been pushing gaming forward, across Xbox and Windows. From the silicon at the heart of our consoles and handhelds, to technologies like DirectX, Advanced Shader Delivery, and AutoSR that helps developers get more from the hardware and deliver better experiences for our players."
"Today, we're excited to take another step forward together. With FSR 4.1 coming to Xbox. Now, we've worked very closely with AMD to optimize this technology, giving developers another powerful tool for great performance and visual quality for players. Now, whether you're playing on an Xbox Ally handheld, as well as coming soon to Xbox Series X and Series S consoles. And this is just the beginning. Our teams are continuing to work together across hardware and software, and there's even more ahead with Project Helix, leveraging FSR Diamond to power what comes next."
It's unclear exactly when these technologies will roll out to Xbox devices. It sounds as though FSR 4.1 will hit Xbox Ally X before the year end, but Xbox Series X|S are listed as "coming soon," with no exact window offered.
Sadly, it seems the Xbox Ally base model is fully incompatible with FSR 4.1, which is a bit of a shame, but it should prove transformative for those with the Xbox Ally X and the just-released Xbox Ally X20 , as well as the Xbox Series S.
UPDATE: I stand corrected, I just confirmed that it is also coming to the Xbox Ally base model as well!
The Xbox Series S has historically been difficult for developers owing to its irregular RAM allocation, but if FSR 4.1 can do some of the heavy lifting, it should ease the pressure on developers to deliver a native 1080p image.
UPDATE: ROGAllyLife is reporting that FSR 4.1 will arrive in preview via the Armoury Crate on October 23, 2026 for Xbox Ally devices, with a new toggle in the Command Center. It will reportedly support over 400+ games that currently support FSR 3.1, adding big performance gains across the board.

articles.title_zh: PHP RCE Zero-Days CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619 Leak Early
articles.content_orig:
We couldn't find any blog articles matching your search. Try searching for other cybersecurity topics or keywords.
PHP will ship fixes for two leaked critical flaws rated CVSS v4.0 9.2 on October 21 at 14:00 UTC, a day before the embargo was set to lift.
Sulochana is a staff writer and technology contributor at Cyber Kendra, covering the latest tech news, cybersecurity, and digital insights.
The PHP security team said on Tuesday that it will ship a security release on Wednesday, October 21, to fix two critical vulnerabilities, after information about the embargoed flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, leaked online.
In an advance notice on php.net, the team said the release is scheduled for 14:00 UTC, which is 10:00 a.m. ET and 19:30 IST. It rated both vulnerabilities 9.2 under CVSS v4.0 and urged all PHP users to prepare now so they can upgrade as soon as the builds are available. The PHP Foundation shared the same notice on X.
The PHP team said full details, affected versions, and fixed versions will be published with the release. It also said it may ship earlier if details of either flaw become public or if evidence of active exploitation emerges.
Wednesday is a day earlier than the date researchers under embargo had been working to. Security firm watchTowr said everyone had been supposed to wait until Thursday at 11:00 a.m. ET, and the first public report of the leak pointed to October 22.
That report came in a “Tell HN” post on Hacker News at 15:20 UTC on October 20. Citing a “reliable source”, user petecooper wrote that two PHP remote code execution flaws rated CVSS 10.0 were due for disclosure, affecting all PHP versions from PHP 5 onwards. The poster admitted having no evidence, and the post was later flagged, but screenshots were already circulating on X and Mastodon.
watchTowr then confirmed the leak, saying the information concerned zero-day RCE vulnerabilities in PHP. “We can confirm that they’re real,” the company said, adding that it could not share more and urging administrators to patch once fixes are out.
We were all supposed to wait until Thursday at 11am ET. Information has leaked wrt zero-day embargoed RCE vulns in PHP. We can confirm that they're real. CVE-2926-109618/619 We cannot share further information right now. Take this seriously and apply patches when available. pic.twitter.com/kguM8fpq13
Security researcher Florian Roth wrote on X that the flaw is an RCE in PHP core and that only PHP 8 will receive patches. PHP 5 and PHP 7 reached end of life years ago, so servers still running them would stay exposed without an official fix. Nicolas Krassas said he will publish a hands-on lab once the embargo lifts, and Kevin Beaumont flagged the leak on Mastodon .
The official severity differs from the leak. PHP rates both bugs 9.2 under CVSS v4.0, while the leaked posts cited 10.0 and did not say which version of the scoring system they used. The PHP notice does not name the CVE IDs or describe the bugs as code execution flaws; those details come from watchTowr and the leaked reports.
No technical details have been made public. Both CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 remain in reserved status, and none of the posts identify the affected function, extension, or configuration. In an FAQ on the flaws , watchTowr said it had seen no exploitation in the wild, that the bugs are not in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and no workaround exists before the patch.
An embargo is a private window during which a vendor coordinates fixes with Linux distributions, hosting providers, and security firms, so that patched builds ship at the same moment as the advisory. Once the severity and date leaked, anyone already holding the bugs knew how long they had before fixes landed.
PHP powers WordPress, Drupal, Magento, and most shared hosting, and many site owners rely on their hosting provider to deploy new PHP builds. Xbox senior business strategy manager Brandon Stirrup is tired of pussyfooting around about AI: In a thread on X his week, he said that he wants the world to know that Xbox uses it, that he thinks everyone should be using it, and that he believes so strongly in the cause that he's willing to "take the hit" for saying so.
He has since deleted his X account. A source at Xbox tells PC Gamer that Stirrup opted to deactivate the account because of the volume of replies he was receiving.
Stirrup kicked off his thread on October 18 with a simple message saying he'd "vibe coded a bad but improvable game" over two days, although he only "actively" worked on it for about three hours. "I'm telling you I tried it and it's true…anyone can build a game."
After saying that developers and studios who aren't incorporating AI into their strategies are "planning for a fake future," Stirrup went all in.
"Look if I'm fired tomorrow it will be because I told you the truth that nobody wants you to know. You can make a game with a simple prompt and yes you can make custom, tailored games. Everything you want in a game is right there for the taking, for better or worse," he wrote.
"I'm happy to take the hit if it means hundreds at Xbox can stop pretending that they're not using AI. It's time to accept and move forward."
After calling out the game industry and gamers alike for their reluctance to accept "reality," Stirrup stated explicitly that Xbox is "using AI" and then added, "My goal is to get this over with so we can move on as a company, despite the fact that some will persecute me for this: we use AI, just as all companies do in 2026."
Credit: Brandon Stirrup (Twitter)
There's a growing push for people to simply accept the "reality" of AI: Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, for instance, recently said the studio was "moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration," after which the Epic Games Store ignited a firestorm by saying it " vibe coded " its new launcher. Xbox, now under the leadership of a former AI executive, recently launched a new Xbox Labs program to pursue emerging technologies, which naturally includes AI; even Linux recently dropped its rule requiring AI usage disclosures .
Stirrup himself is an enthusiastic AI evangelist: Last month, he also counselled laid-off employees to use Copilot to catalog their skills and accomplishments at the company.

articles.title_orig: Does anyone actually want to win the medium-lift race in the United States?
articles.title_zh: Does anyone actually want to win the medium-lift race in the United States?
articles.content_orig:
It has been 13 years since the debut of a new medium-lift rocket in the United States, the Antares vehicle developed by Orbital Sciences Corporation.
The initial 100-series variant of the Antares rocket was kind of a hot mess. The rocket used old Soviet engines built during the era when Apollo astronauts were landing on the Moon. Decades later, in the 1990s, Aerojet acquired the engines and refurbished them for a rocket that would launch in the 2010s. Predictably, on the fifth launch of an Antares rocket in 2014, it exploded.
The Antares vehicle is the last of a dying breed of medium-lift rockets—defined as having a lift capacity of 2 to 20 metric tons—in the United States. Nearly a decade and a half later there is a new generation of medium-lift vehicles coming online, and they are starkly different from Antares, which had not just Russian engines but a core stage manufactured in Ukraine.
Four forthcoming rockets all have engines built by the rocket’s manufacturer in the United States. Each of these companies has taken various lessons from SpaceX’s successful Falcon 9 rocket, arguably the most important of which is to build as much of one’s rocket, and particularly the engines, in-house as possible to control timelines and costs.
Now, with SpaceX pulling the Falcon 9 rocket from the commercial market as soon as 2028, the “race” to bring new medium-lift capacity into service is for more than bragging rights. There are fortunes to be made, and commercial space startups to be saved.
Satellite operators legitimately don’t know who to book launches with in the 2027 to 2030 timeframe because of uncertainty over which rockets will be available. The Falcon 9 is no longer for sale. The larger Vulcan and New Glenn rockets have stacked manifests and are expensive for small- and medium-sized satellites. And no one really knows which new medium-lift vehicles will be ready and capable of scaling up their launch cadence.
With all of this in mind, Ars Technica is here to help with a guide to the medium-lift space race in the United States, along with some (almost certainly wrong) predictions on when the rockets may debut. The list below is in our expected order of launch. Disagree? Feel free to shame us in the comments. And if you’re an engineer or technician working on one of these projects, keep going. This stuff is really hard and we salute your dedication. Prove us wrong!
The smallest of the medium-lift rockets under development, with a capacity of 3 tons in fully reusable mode and 7 tons in expendable mode, the Nova rocket is also arguably the most ambitious.
That’s because the rocket aims for full reusability, with a novel upper stage thruster design and heat shield to solve the difficult problem of protecting a vehicle reentering at orbital velocity. Additionally, the first-stage engines are full-flow staged combustion, which is ambitious for a first engine design.
Despite all of this, the rocket is making credible progress toward liftoff. The Nova rocket’s first stage is nearly complete at its factory in Kent, Washington. Last week Stoke shipped the second stage of Nova to its test site, and if hot-fire tests are successful it will move to the launch site. The launch complex at Cape Canaveral, Florida, is nearly complete.
Recently, for the first time, Stoke began to publicly talk about a date for Nova’s debut. The company is targeting “early” 2027 for launch. That’s probably optimistic, but we could see a late spring or summer debut.
Predicted launch debut : July 2027
Technically, this is not a medium-lift rocket. The company is advertising up to 33.5 metric tons to low-Earth orbit in fully expendable mode for Terran R. But new rockets rarely hit their advertised lift capacity early in their lifetime, and with a reusable first stage (which is necessary for the economics of Terran R to close), the lift capacity is closer to 20 metric tons.
Nevertheless, this is a large and ambitious project. And it was pretty much left for dead until former Google Chief Executive Eric Schmidt acquired the company a year and a half ago. Schmidt has injected much-needed funding into Relativity, and sources report that morale at the Long Beach, California-based company has improved significantly.
In recent months the company has reported some notable progress. It completed acceptance testing for all 13 of the Aeon R engines that will power its first stage, qualified the first stage structures, and is making progress on assembly of the first stage. Then, last Friday, the company said the Terran R’s second stage had successfully completed its first integrated hot fire test.
Stoke and Relativity are fairly close to one another in their development timelines. Relativity is ahead in second stage testing, but Stoke has a lead in launch site readiness. I am going to give the slight edge to the smaller rocket in terms of being ready for launch.
Predicted launch debut : September 2027
With a lift capacity of between 8.5 and 15 metric tons, depending on first stage reuse and landing site, Rocket Lab’s Neutron rocket slots somewhere in between Nova and Terran R.
For a long time it appeared as though Neutron would become the first new medium-lift rocket to debut since Antares, but the vehicle has had some teething pains: Rocket Lab has experienced some problems with the Archimedes engine , and more recently the company revealed some challenges with carbon-fiber domes.
The Neutron rocket’s first stage is the “largest pressurized structure ever made out of carbon composite,” Rocket Lab chief Peter Beck said this month. “Because of its scale, we’ve had to develop new out-of-autoclave processes to build Neutron, and this includes custom cure cycles for the very large pieces, like the forward and aft domes for the propellant tanks on Stage One.”
That doesn’t sound particularly easy. Given the lack of flight hardware in evidence, we’re not sure the company meets its latest launch target, which is now sometime in 2027.
Predicted launch debut : January 2028
We began this article with the Antares rocket, which was developed by Orbital Sciences. That company was later acquired by Northrop Grumman. A few years ago, seeking a home-grown alternative to Antares, Northrop announced a partnership with Firefly to co-develop the Eclipse rocket .
Firefly is developing the Miranda engines that will power Eclipse’s first stage, and this work appears to be progressing well. But there has been little public talk about development of the first and second stage hardware that will be built around the Miranda engine. Similar to Rocket Lab, Firefly and Northrop are also working with carbon-composite structures, so there may be some challenges there.
The partnership between Firefly, a new space company, and Northrop, a traditional space company, is also likely to produce some friction. It is difficult to make an educated guess on Eclipse because there is so much uncertainty about the rocket’s development. Typically, that means things aren’t going well or quickly. For now, we’re leaning toward pessimism.
Predicted launch debut : NET 2029

Estimated read time: 3-4 minutes
SALT LAKE CITY — If you've been watching mortgage rates and telling yourself you'll buy when they come down, you might want to think again.
Jennifer Yeo is with Presidio Real Estate and knows the market inside and out. She shared a reality check on the real estate market.
We've gotten used to incredibly low mortgage rates over the past few years.
"We don't wanna soon forget the historical lows of twos and threes," Yeo said. "If you look back over the last 50 years, our average interest rate was about 8%."
Those unusually low rates changed our expectations. Compared to recent history, today's rates feel expensive. Compared to more long-term history, they're actually much closer to normal. Yeo said we shouldn't make decisions based solely on the hope that rates will fall.
"I don't see it changing anytime soon," she said. "There are a lot of other things you could do to be in this market."
Yeo said many buyers spend so much time watching rates that they overlook factors they can actually control.
"People focus on the interest rate so much, but that's just one factor of having buying power," she explained.
She suggested talking with a lender to figure out what payment fits comfortably into your budget.
"Find out what your mortgage payment looks like and what's comfortable for you," Yeo said.
We can't control national interest rates, but Yeo said we can influence other parts of the lending equation.
"The things we can control are your credit, your debt to income, things like that," she said.
Those factors play an important role in determining borrowing power and financing options. She also pointed out that you have more options available than you might realize.
"Builders are buying rates down, sellers are buying some rates down for people," Yeo explained. "There's a couple things you can do when it comes to the interest rate."
While rates matter, they're not the only tool available.
A big advantage of the current market is minimal competition. Yeo mentioned the frenzy of 2020 and 2021 when historically low rates led to bidding wars.
"We had multiple offers and paying over appraised value and things like that," she said. "Right now there's a lot of opportunity in this market. There's way less competition."
Entering the market now could give you stronger negotiating power and better terms.
One strategy Yeo said to explore is a rate buydown.
"It's a great opportunity right now," she said. "The sellers are doing it. A lot of builders are doing it."
A rate buydown allows money from a seller or builder incentive to be applied toward lowering the buyer's mortgage rate.
"Basically take it off the price of the home and put it towards it, so they buy down your rate," Yeo explained. "You can get them down to, like, a 4% right now."
She recommended asking questions and investigating all your available options before ruling yourself out of the market.
Buyers aren't the only ones navigating a changing market. With more inventory and more choices available, sellers may need to offer incentives to stand out.
"If you're a seller in this market, get motivated," Yeo said. "You might have to share some of your equity with the buyers in this market, because there's so many options out there."
The environment has become more balanced, which means both sides need realistic expectations.
Yeo emphasized that markets don't look obvious until they're in the past.
"I am a betting woman, and I bet there's going to be millions of people that wish they would've bought in this market," she said. "Historically ... our values have increased nonstop for the last 50 years."
Yeo said to get informed about the current market.
"Talk to an educated realtor, talk to an educated lender," she said. "Find out what opportunities are out there for you."

articles.title_zh: YouTube starts hiding the dislike button on normal videos
articles.content_orig:
After removing dislike counts years ago, new UI tests at YouTube are making it harder to even using the dislike button at all.
In 2021, YouTube removed the dislike count as a way to “de-weaponize” the button – effort that had been ongoing for years – with YouTube even acknowledging that it was a decision that users might disagree with. Now, following similar changes to Shorts , YouTube appears to be testing further hiding the dislike button.
A report on Twitter/X highlighted by Neowin showcases YouTube hiding the dislike button under an overflow menu, hiding it from view despite the like button remaining front and center. This appears to be on the desktop website, though we couldn’t replicate the same behavior on our end.
It’s not the only case of this happening, though.
Over the past couple of weeks, reports on Reddit have seen the dislike button vanish, with another web user seeing a slightly different UI to the one above, but with the same result of offloading the button to an overflow menu alongside the “Report” button.
YouTube runs tests like this frequently, but given the same change was made to the dislike button on Shorts several months ago, it’s all but certain that the same will happen to standard videos.

articles.title_zh: China’s Long Shadow over Washington’s Russian Diesel Deal
articles.content_orig:
On October 9, the US Treasury issued General License 135 (GL135), authorizing transactions involving Russian-origin diesel until April 7, 2027. On October 13, just four days after GL135 was issued, a tanker transporting roughly 40,000 tonnes of ultra-low-sulfur diesel was en route from the Baltic port of Primorsk toward Morocco. The destination of this shipment was not coincidental either, with the African country having struggled to procure diesel and petrol since the start of the Iran war.
In this sense, GL135 changes the economic calculus for countries that have had to keep their energy ties with Moscow politically or commercially opaque in order to preserve their traditionally close relation with the US and avoid straining relations with the EU. Moreover, the Moroccan case suggests that international sanctions regimes may have limited leverage over third countries once the threat of US enforcement is removed . So, although many US allies were already importing fuel from Russia (Figure 1), GL135 will affect the steep discount and simplify the logistic arrangements that characterized those transactions.
Therefore, the likeliest near-term consequence of GL135 is rerouting barrels that might otherwise have gone elsewhere to US-aligned countries and, possibly, reducing the discount at which Russian diesel traded because of sanctions-related risks, although global supply barely budges . In other words, two seemingly contradictory outcomes can coexist: the pressure on regions struggling to source fuel may ease as diesel shipments from Russia become easier to arrange and reach more buyers, yet the global market balance changes little. Still, the less discussed question is whether easier access to Russian diesel may have been deemed necessary to weaken Chinaâs leverage over fuel-short buyers.
The origins of GL135 should be understood through the interaction between US domestic political pressure and global market imbalances. Indeed, US domestic politics may itself be partly a consequence of the global diesel supply shock, given that disruptions to shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have contributed to US retail diesel prices reaching levels not seen since 2008. Nevertheless, the timing makes the domestic political dimension difficult to ignore: the move came weeks before the midterm elections, when high diesel prices had become a political liability for Republicans.
The geoeconomic rationale behind GL135 is potentially even more relevant, albeit less discussed. Over the summer, China helped cap oil prices by limiting its imports of crude and, given a supply shock is now hitting another market tightly linked to that for oil, one could have expected Beijing to help stabilize the global economy again. Not least because Chinese commercial inventories of middle distillates, a category including diesel and jet fuel, are down just 8.4% from October 2025 . However, Chinaâs willingness to mitigate the crude-supply shock correlated with a different set of market circumstances, not least the USâs ability to increase production to avoid domestic shocks and alleviate scarcity through its strategic reserves. Instead, this time China is prioritizing its energy security by shoring up its strategic reserves and by restricting and tightly managing diesel exports. As a result, Beijing commands enough refining capacity to â bail out the diesel marketâ and it has acquired new leverage over fuel-importing countries that are increasingly exposed to its supply decisions.

Meanwhile, the US has not increased its supply enough to help the Philippines , Morocco , Tunisia , and other allies struggling to secure enough fuel to keep their economy running (Figure 2). Not least because rising prices at home reflect the level of US commercial inventories of refined petroleum products, which are over 10 million barrels lower than last year and regional stocks are up to 32% below the 2021-25 seasonal average. Crucially, the US has got less leverage in the diesel market than for crude, where releases from the strategic reserves and increased output can readily materialize. Moreover, a rapid increase in domestic refining is unlikely given that US refineries are already operating close to the mid-90% in utilization and there is no idle capacity that can come online on short notice. Rather, declining stocks are chiefly due to the closure or conversion to biofuel of several refineries across the country partly motivated by âgreenâ policies. According to one estimate, seven major closures and conversions have removed roughly 1.235 million barrels per day of US refining capacity, more than 6.5% of the total, making external supply disruptions more consequential.
Seen in this context, GL135 appears not just as an electoral maneuver, but also as an effort to reduce Chinese leverage on global diesel supplies by allowing buyers facing prohibitive prices to tap more openly into Russiaâs exports. However, the move will not materially balance the global diesel balance because the binding constraint remains operational refining capacity. Moreover, Moscow does not appear able to release large quantities of diesel into the market, let alone enough to match the scale of Chinaâs reduced exports, given that Ukraine continues to carry out attacks on Russian refineries. Still, the case of Morocco offers an early indication that removing sanctions on Russian diesel may grant some US allies temporary relief from domestic and regional diesel shortages even if the global market imbalance is not corrected any time soon and Russian refining capacity does not recover .
Having settled the origins of GL135, the next question is who benefits from the rerouting of hundreds of thousands of tonnes of diesel to buyers in undersupplied fuel markets.
GL135 widens the set of eligible partners from which fuel can be imported by removing the sanction-risk associated with Russian-origin diesel. However, several analysts tend to agree that a mere reallocation of existing barrels cannot solve supply bottlenecks in the diesel market as effectively as a recovery in refinery output in the US and Russia, unblocking traffic through Hormuz, or a liberalization of Chinese diesel exports. So, the answer depends less on the number of Russian barrels being traded than on how the value of those sales is redistributed.
Given that global supply remains insufficient to balance an inelastic demand and even oil producers like Russia and the US have struggled to add refining capacity, as Russian diesel gets rerouted the main near-term effect may instead be a redistribution of profits. The main reason Russian producersâ revenues could grow in the short term is that the sanction risk likely translated into a discount on the sale price of diesel, as it has done for crude oil. These price cuts drove exportersâ netbacks down. To further complicate matters, Russian exporters do not typically pay for insurance and freight, since their oil and fuels are sold on âfree-on-boardâ (FOB) terms, yet the sellerâs netback can still be affected indirectly by changes in freight and insurance. Practically, buyersâ willingness and ability to pay can limit the sellersâ ability to pass freight and insurance costs through and reduce its netback. Hence, the extensive sanctions with which the G7 established for maritime service providers working with Russian oil companies, put further downward pressure on the latterâs netbacks.
In fact, while the product was being sold at a discount, freight cost rose to cover the so-called âshadow-fleet premiumâ that shippers demanded as compensation for the sanctions and compliance risks. So, as long as those sanctions were backed by the threat of US enforcement, including through tariffs , part of the margin that would otherwise have accrued to Russian sellers shifted to logistics operators and intermediaries.

articles.title_orig: China threatens retaliation if U.K. follows the EU on tariffs
articles.title_zh: China threatens retaliation if U.K. follows the EU on tariffs
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — Beijing has threatened to retaliate if the U.K. raises tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, aligning with the European Union.
Responding to POLITICO’s story that Britain was looking to act in “lockstep” with the bloc to counter China’s market dominance in electric cars, a spokesperson from the Chinese Ministry of Commerce said : “If the U.K. insists on imposing restrictions on Chinese electric vehicles, China will resolutely retaliate and safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese industries.”
The U.K. is currently working with its European partners to avoid a 10% electric vehicle tariff from the beginning of next year, when stricter rules of origin under the Brexit trade deal kick in.
The British government is also lobbying to be included in the EU’s Made in Europe policies, which give Brussels-made products preferential treatment in certain procurement projects.
U.K. Trade Minister Anas Sarwar told POLITICO on the sidelines of the German-British Business Summit at Mansion House last week that “the more that the U.K. and the EU work together and act in lockstep, the better it is for both the U.K. and the European Union.”
“The automotive sector and partnership remain strong, but do we have to grapple with the challenge that comes from rapid expansion in China? Of course we do,” he added.
China urged Britain to follow World Trade Organization rules and warned it against copying Brussels’ approach, arguing that tariffs on Chinese EVs would be discriminatory.
“China urges the U.K. to abide by WTO rules, think carefully, and not follow the European Union,” said the Chinese Ministry of Commerce spokesperson. “China will closely monitor the U.K.’s developments.”

articles.title_orig: Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 300 people, sources say
articles.title_zh: Sudan army drones hit mourners and fuel market killing more than 300 people, sources say
articles.content_orig:
Witness says drone struck twice at transport hub in al-Dibab, in one of deadliest single attacks of war
A drone strike near a market in southern Sudan on Sunday evening killed 80 people, mostly commuters catching rides home.
Ahmed Wadi, a witness, said the attack in the town of al-Dibab in West Kordofan state left “50 bodies who I helped bury, one of them my own brother Mohamed”.
Using a satellite internet connection to circumvent a communications blackout, Wadi also said 47 other people were transported to the nearest town, al-Mujlad. A medical source, requesting anonymity for his safety, said 30 of them died from their injuries.
The medic said: “A total of 80 people were killed in the drone strike on al-Dibab, and another drone strike on al-Mujlad injured four who are currently being treated.”
Wadi said the drone struck twice, 10 minutes apart, “on a transport hub where people gather to travel back to their villages after the market day ends”.
The attack is one of the deadliest single strikes since war broke out in April 2023 when a power struggle between the Sudanese armed forces (SAF), headed by Gen Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo , erupted into violence in the capital, Khartoum.
The RSF-declared administration, known as Tasis, accused the army of carrying out Sunday’s strike. All of West Kordofan state is under RSF control.
Sudan has witnessed an escalation in the use of drones in the war. Between January and April, drone strikes accounted for at least 880 civilian deaths, more than 80% of all conflict-related civilian deaths in Sudan.
After drone strikes on a busy livestock market in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur state, on Friday, the SAF said they had killed RSF fighters, but the RSF accused the military of killing 30 civilians.
The fighting in Sudan has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced many more. It has been fuelled by foreign powers with vested interests who are supporting sides in the conflict.
Last week, Rosemary DiCarlo, the undersecretary-general for political and peacebuilding affairs at the UN, warned the security council that the conflict and humanitarian crisis was deteriorating “with no breakthrough on the horizon”.
She said: “They [the warring parties] are not moving closer to dialogue. On the contrary, they seem to believe that they can make greater gains on the battlefield and that continued external support will allow them to pursue their objectives by force.”

articles.title_orig: China-Laos air base could be another Southeast Asian forward outpost for Beijing
articles.title_zh: China-Laos air base could be another Southeast Asian forward outpost for Beijing
articles.content_orig:
A new joint military training facility in Laos could give Beijing a lasting foothold in mainland Southeast Asia even without an immediate boost to its combat power, analysts told Radio Free Asia.
Beijing and Vientiane opened a joint support and training center and an aviation academy at Ban Keun, about 50 kilometers north of the Lao capital, on Sept. 29. Beijing says the facility will train Lao air force pilots and it will be maintained by both countries.
The airfield, once complete, would be China’s second joint military outpost in Southeast Asia, after a Chinese-funded expansion of Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base opened in April of last year. The facility at Ream, despite its official designation as a dual-use facility, has seen a regular rotation of Chinese naval vessels.
The joint facility in Laos could allow China to deepen military ties, familiarize personnel with overseas operations and lay the groundwork for a larger presence, Joseph Kristanto, a research analyst at Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, told RFA.
“Ultimately, I think the more important question is not simply whether Ban Keun could accommodate Chinese military aircraft, but whether Beijing intends to develop the facility into a sustained operational hub,” he said.
China’s Defense Ministry said in an announcement that the facility would be maintained by both countries and was “not directed against any third party.” It said its construction and use complied with domestic and international law and would strengthen military cooperation and support regional peace and stability.
Laos’ state news agency KPL reported that officials from both countries described the project at the opening ceremony as the product of cooperation based on mutual respect and equality. The facility would develop Lao military pilots’ practical skills, it said.
The KPL report also said both sides pledged to expand cooperation through joint training and exercises, personnel development and humanitarian assistance. Neither that report nor the Chinese announcement specified how many Chinese military personnel would work at Ban Keun, how long they would remain or the conditions governing Chinese aircraft deployments.
Satellite imagery analysis provided to RFA suggests some construction continued after the opening of the joint airfield. But its future military significance will depend on more than its physical completion, including the extent of Chinese access and the frequency and nature of activities there, Kristanto said.
China already operates military facilities on disputed features in the South China Sea. Ban Keun could extend its overseas presence inland, offering opportunities to build closer ties with the Lao military and gain experience operating from a foreign facility, he said.
The airfield’s immediate military advantages are less clear, analysts said. China has airbases in its own southern territory closer to the South China Sea, raising questions about what additional operations an inland facility in Laos would enable.
In satellite imagery of the airfield during its opening, eight aircraft are visible. Private satellite imagery analyst Jacob Bogle told RFA they were K-8, also known as JL-8, light attack and training aircraft.
Examining an Oct. 7 image, he identified what he thought was one remaining aircraft, while cautioning that the image was blurry. He suggested the others had likely moved into hangars, although their locations could not be established from that observation.
Bogle also identified what appeared to be workshops and temporary construction infrastructure beside the southern end of the runway.
“So while the runway and main buildings are completed, it looks like there is still some minor work that is being finished,” he said.
The imagery does not establish who owns or operates the aircraft. Both China and Laos operate the K-8 type, according to analysts cited by Reuters.
But a Lao military officer, while downplaying concerns over increased Chinese military presence in Southeast Asia, confirmed to RFA that at least some of the fighter jets at the facility are Chinese.
“It is a pilot training airport. A group of people are envious that Laos has a flight training center, yet Laos has never complained about neighboring countries hosting U.S. air bases,” said the officer on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak on such matters.
“When Laos built Ban Keun Airport for pilot training, some people overreacted. Naturally, Chinese officials brought their own fighter jets, given that it is a joint Lao-Chinese operation,” he said.
Bogle said it was too early to determine China’s future position at Ban Keun, but that the facility warranted monitoring.
Kristanto said operating combat aircraft from Laos would require substantial investment in fuel storage, maintenance facilities, munitions, air defense and other supporting infrastructure.
“At present, I see little evidence that Ban Keun offers a decisive operational advantage over China’s existing facilities,” he said.
Such limitations do not rule out a broader role in the future. Ban Keun could theoretically support intelligence gathering, surveillance, logistics or forward aircraft deployments if the necessary infrastructure and access arrangements were established, he said.
A sustained Chinese military presence in Laos could add another consideration for neighboring Vietnam, which already faces China across its northern land border and contests Beijing’s claims in the South China Sea.
China’s expansive maritime claims overlap with the exclusive economic zones of Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia, Brunei and Indonesia. Vietnam also claims the Paracel and Spratly island groups, where competing sovereignty claims are distinct from disputes over rights to surrounding waters. China controls the Paracels, while several governments occupy features in the Spratlys.
In 2016, an international arbitral tribunal rejected China’s claims to the entire South China Sea based on its controversial nine-dash line, which surrounds the whole sea. This claim was seen to exceed what Beijing could legally claim under the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea.
Beijing rejected the decision, and has continued to assert its claims over areas that are within the exclusive economic zones of the other claimants.
China has strengthened this position through island-building and military infrastructure, including runways, surveillance equipment and air defenses on occupied reefs. Those facilities support a wider maritime presence in waters where rival claimants seek to protect fishing grounds, energy resources and access to their outposts.
Ban Keun would introduce a different geographic consideration for Hanoi, potentially bringing Chinese military activity to its western side as well.
Bogle argued that facilities in Laos and Cambodia, together with China’s South China Sea bases, had effectively encircled Vietnam.
Kristanto was more cautious. Vietnam would have to account for the possibility of a Chinese military presence beyond its northern border and the South China Sea, he said, but Ban Keun’s inland location and China’s existing airbases limit its immediate operational value.
“For now, I would characterize Ban Keun as a potentially important strategic foothold rather than a major shift in the regional military balance.”
China’s involvement at Cambodia’s Ream naval base shows why a facility’s use over time can be more revealing than its designation as a joint training center, the analysts said.
China financed an expansion of Ream, on Cambodia’s southern coast, where its joint support and training center opened in April 2025. Cambodia maintains that Chinese personnel and warships are not permanently based there.

articles.title_orig: China built more than twice naval tonnage of US in 2024-25: Euronaval
articles.title_zh: China built more than twice naval tonnage of US in 2024-25: Euronaval
articles.content_orig:
PARIS — China built more than twice the naval tonnage of the United States in the 2024-25 period, narrowing the gap between the two countries’ navies, according to the World Defense Shipbuilding report published by Euronaval ahead of the 2026 edition of the naval defense show.
The combined tonnage of combat ships built by China in the two years through to December 2025 amounted to 636,208 tons, compared to 270,509 tons for the United States, according to data compiled by Flottes de Combat and French maritime industry association Gican.
China accounted for more than a third of the global naval tonnage constructed in 2024-25, based on the Euronaval report. U.S. lawmakers and congressional researchers have warned that China’s greater shipbuilding capacity, combined with delays and bottlenecks in U.S. naval shipbuilding, could hurt America’s ability to keep up with Beijing’s expanding fleet.
“We are seeing a fairly substantial expansion of naval forces, and consequently of shipbuilding,” said Philippe Missoffe, the general director of Gican, in a press briefing here on Tuesday. “We’re seeing an increase in power capabilities, particularly nuclear-powered attack submarines for example.”
Global naval construction overall was booming in the period, with 1.47 million tons of combat vessels built in 2024-25, compared with 959,671 tons in the prior two years. The value of global naval construction amounted to $123.9 billion, climbing from $81.8 billion in 2022-23.
The value of Chinese combat-vessel construction was US$43.5 billion in the latest two-year period, compared with $26.8 billion for the U.S., the report said.
China has reversed roles from 2022-2023, when production of the country’s naval yards amounted to 202,520 tons, compared with 245,703 tons for the U.S., according to the previous edition of the shipbuilding report published in 2024.
The U.S. fleet of combat vessels of more than 200 tons amounted to 3.11 million tons as of Jan. 1, 2026, compared to 1.44 million tons for China’s fleet, the report showed, That compares with 3.22 million tons for the U.S. and 1.3 million tons for China two years earlier.
Russia was in third place in terms of naval construction in 2024-25, with 149,056 tons built, followed by India with 76,430 tons and Italy with 53,700 tons. Turkey, France, Japan, South Korean and Romania rounded out the top 10 of naval builders.
The four-day Euronaval show, the world’s biggest maritime-defense exhibition, is set to kick of in Paris on Nov. 3. The number of exhibitors will be more than 40% higher than in 2024, according to the organizers.
Rudy Ruitenberg is a Europe correspondent for Defense News. He started his career at Bloomberg News and has experience reporting on technology, commodity markets and politics.

The Government Service Network (GSN) reported a surge of 185.6 million cyberattacks in July, suggesting that Beijing could be preparing large-scale interference operations ahead of the Nov. 28 elections, government officials said.
Cyberattacks on the network, likely originating in China, spiked between June and last month, the National Security Bureau (NSB) said in a report submitted to the Legislative Yuan for a meeting scheduled for tomorrow.
As of last month, the GSN was attacked 2.58 million times a day on average, and the attacks reported in July exceeded the sum of total cyberattacks in the first quarter this year, the document said.
Cyberattacks exceeded 100 million in three months last year: during the anniversary of President William Lai’s (賴清德) inauguration in April (100 million), in May (about 300 million) and during Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim’s (蕭美琴) visit to Europe in November (about 200 million), it said.
The NSB cannot rule out the possibility that the July attacks are part of Beijing’s plan to meddle in next month’s nine-in-one elections, the report said, adding that the agency had warned of the same in April.
Chinese hackers in the first half of the year targeted academic institutions, telecommunications and defense industry supply chains as part of a long war against Taiwan’s critical infrastructure, it said.
The attacks were aimed at disrupting Taiwan’s ability to govern and direct national defense policy, its collaboration with other governments and the theft of sensitive technology, it said.
Beijing-directed cyberwarfare continues to improve in sophistication and artificial intelligence (AI) technology has been deployed in hacks, it said.
AI is utilized across various stages of a cyberattack, including probing for weaknesses, target seeking, searching for zero-day exploits and malware attacks via e-mail, the report said.
Automation has increased Chinese hackers’ operational tempo and their efficiency in finding gaps in Taiwan’s defenses and identifying targets for infiltration, it said.
Meanwhile, the NSB said it believes that Beijing would leverage technology and human intelligence to craft a strategy to influence next month’s elections, targeting Taiwan’s domestic wedge issues such as energy, food safety and national defense, and using fake polls and reports about the races, and AI-generated content, it said.
Suspicious social media accounts made 2.5 million posts containing controversial or disputed information from January to last month, up 48 percent compared with 1.69 million in the same period last year, the report said.
The method and platform for spreading cognitive warfare posts included content farms, AI-generated video or audio content, and brigading the comment section on platforms, forums and other Web sites, it said.
Facebook and Threads accounted for 68.9 percent and 9 percent respectively of all controversial content from suspicious accounts, it said.
Suspicious posts on Facebook and Threads were up by 25.3 and 4.5 percentage points from last year respectively, indicating China’s increasing preference for using these platforms, the report said.
AI is playing an increasingly prominent role in Beijing’s informational operations, it said.
China’s strategy for manipulating Taiwanese public opinion follows the model of using official outlets to craft narratives, which are then amplified by troll, bot and public relations company-owned accounts, the report said.

articles.title_orig: Trump Tariffs on Canada Spark Latest Lawsuit Over Trade Powers
articles.title_zh: Trump Tariffs on Canada Spark Latest Lawsuit Over Trade Powers
articles.content_orig:
A new lawsuit filed Tuesday challenges President Donald Trump 's invocation of a Depression-era law to impose 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods .
Trump in July used Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to slap those steep tariffs on Canadian hockey sticks, wine, honey, wigs, and other products in response to alleged trade discrimination by Ottawa. It was the first time the 96-year-old law had ever been used to impose a tariff.
"Section 338 is a relic of the retaliation-based tariff policy" that has been "impliedly repealed" by subsequent legislation, the civil complaint filed in the U.S. Court of International Trade says.
The suit was filed by Gellert Global Group, a New Jersey-based food importer that says its cheeses are covered by the tariffs. The complaint asks the court to declare the tariffs unlawful, block their enforcement, and order the Trump administration to issue refunds for duties already paid, with interest.
Gellert Global is represented by the Liberty Justice Center, the same legal group that dealt a major blow to Trump's trade agenda by successfully contesting his "reciprocal" tariffs.
The Supreme Court struck those tariffs down in February. The administration is in the process of refunding the estimated $166 billion that the federal government collected from importers through the reciprocal duties.
The Liberty Justice Center is currently engaged in two other lawsuits against what it says is Trump's misuse of laws to impose sweeping tariffs.
"This case is not about the president. It is about the presidency," the group's CEO Sara Albrecht said in a statement Tuesday morning announcing Gellert Global's suit. "No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required."
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on the suit.

articles.title_orig: You Should Probably Check Your Google Home Speaker’s Data Usage
articles.title_zh: You Should Probably Check Your Google Home Speaker’s Data Usage
articles.content_orig:
The new Google Home Speaker has an issue where it downloads hundreds of gigabytes of data in the background for some owners.
Over the past week, several reports have emerged about how the Google Home Speaker appears to be continuously downloading data from company servers.
In my case, a Google Home Speaker that has not been used in the past day for voice commands or media streaming consumed 17 GB of data in 24 hours. At 3 a.m. PT, it downloaded 9.99 GB. Given the timing, this could be related to failed attempts to download device firmware.
Meanwhile, on October 13, the same speaker downloaded 41 GB of data. Over the past 30 days, the total download comes in at 132 GB.
It’s not clear if this is a widespread issue. Another lightly used Home Speaker of ours (in a different household) downloaded only 2 GB of data in the past month.
That doesn't make sense how much storage does it have? It's just downloading and deleting constantly?
Most routers let you check how much data a particular device has used. If you’re using Nest Wifi, go to the Google Home app’s Wifi top tab > Devices > select your speaker > Device usage graphs. You can switch between 1-, 7-, and 30-day graphs.
We’re not seeing this download issue with other Google Home and Nest devices, including several Nest Hubs in the same house as the affected Home Speaker.
If you have multiple Home Speakers and a limited data plan, this issue could easily breach your cap, as some have found.
In a statement to 9to5Google today, the company acknowledged the issue and said “a fix is already rolling out that should address this for users.”

articles.title_zh: Pending home sales sink to 25-year low as buyers flee high mortgage rates
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Homebuyers are backing out of contracts at near-record rates, a potential sign of how higher mortgage rates are prompting buyers to rethink their plans.
Nationwide, 14.5% of homes fell out of contract in September, according to Redfin data, the highest share on record apart from the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Read more: Why the housing market is in for 'a challenging couple months'
Homes can fall out of contract for a number of reasons, such as inspection findings or financing pitfalls, or when a buyer just has a change of heart. But pending sales tend to fall through at higher rates when buyers have more options and more negotiating power, as they currently do in much of the country.
Indeed, metro areas that are notably buyer's markets, like Jacksonville and Tampa, Fla., and Las Vegas, all had contract cancellation rates approaching 20%, higher than anywhere else in the country. But they're relatively rare in strong seller's markets like San Francisco, where just 2.8% of deals fell apart.

articles.title_orig: UK to deploy fighter jets to help Saudis against Houthi attacks
articles.title_zh: UK to deploy fighter jets to help Saudis against Houthi attacks
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — U.K. fighter jets will be sent to aid Saudi Arabia in defending itself against attacks on critical energy and civilian infrastructure by the Houthis.
The Iranian-backed Islamist militia group, based in civil war-hit Yemen, has been launching ballistic missile strikes on Saudi Arabia for the past few weeks, successfully hitting three airports earlier this month.
The Ministry of Defence announced Tuesday that Royal Air Force Typhoon fighters will be deployed to the Gulf Kingdom — while stressing that they will be only used in a defensive capacity.
U.K. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the “continuing attacks” on the U.K.’s ally are “absolutely despicable.”
“The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region,” he added, referencing the attacks earlier this month that killed 14 people and injured hundreds more.
Streeting said that the fighter jets will be used to protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles. The U.K. will also send an Atlas A400M aircraft, used to transport the equipment, as well as military advisers.
“This builds on the UK equipment and personnel we already have in the country to defend against Houthi air attacks,” Streeting said.
The MoD argued that there is a link between the conflict in the Persian Gulf and the situation domestically in the U.K., pointing to disrupted energy supplies and a subsequent rise in the cost of living.
Since Prime Minister Andy Burnham arrived in Downing Street in July he has offered more support to Saudi Arabia. In September, he agreed to a request for air-to-air refueling of the country’s jets.
Pressed Tuesday on whether the U.K. risked being sucked into the Saudi war with the Houthis, Burnham’s official spokesperson told reporters: “I don’t accept that characterization. Our support for Saudi Arabia is considered proportionate and focused on helping them defend themselves against relentless Houthi attacks.”
They added: “Regional instability can have a serious impact at home in the U.K. We’re clear it’s in the U.K.’s economic and security interests that the Houthis do not succeed, and our approach is about defending our people, our interests, and our allies.”
